functions.name: moop_feature_id_lookup
functions.comment:
/**
* Run the cross-organism ID lookup for one needle, in one match mode.
*
* $mode is 'exact' (feature_uniquename = ?) or 'version' (GLOB 'needle.*', i.e. the same
* ID carrying any version suffix).
*
* ⚠️ GLOB, deliberately, NOT LIKE. Both express "starts with"; only GLOB keeps the index.
* SQLite's LIKE is case-insensitive by default, so it cannot use the BINARY-collated
* feature_uniquename_idx and degrades to a full covering-index SCAN. Measured on
* Nematostella:
*     = 'NV2t021704001.1'      SEARCH ... (feature_uniquename=?)      0.00s
*     GLOB 'NV2t021704001.*'   SEARCH ... (uniquename>? AND <?)       0.00s
*     LIKE 'NV2t021704001.%'   SCAN  ...                              0.01s
* That gap is small for one database and is the whole cost model for this endpoint, which
* UNION ALLs across EVERY accessible database: a seek stays a seek 85 times over, a scan
* becomes 85 full index scans. Do not "simplify" this to LIKE.
*/

functions.name: addTokensToTrack
addTokenToAdapterUrls
functions.comment:
/**
* Recursively add token parameter to adapter URIs
*
* TOKEN STRATEGY (Updated 2026-02-25 - URL Whitelist):
*
* IMPORTANT: With .htaccess blocking direct file access, ALL requests to
* our tracks servers MUST have JWT tokens, regardless of access_level.
*
* Strategy:
* 1. Trusted servers (in trusted_tracks_servers config)
*    → ALWAYS add token (your servers that validate JWTs)
*    → This includes PUBLIC tracks on your servers!
*
* 2. External servers (not in whitelist, e.g., UCSC, Ensembl)
*    → NEVER add token (they don't validate our JWTs)
*
* 3. MOOP internal paths
*    → ALWAYS add token (routed through tracks.php)
*
* Key Point: access_level controls FILTERING (who sees track in config)
*            URL whitelist controls TOKENS (which servers get tokens)
*
* Examples:
* - PUBLIC track on your server → Token added (for .htaccess bypass)
* - PUBLIC track on UCSC → No token (external public server)
* - COLLABORATOR track on your server → Token added (authenticated access)
* - COLLABORATOR track on UCSC → No token + warning logged (misconfigured)
*
* Each tracks.php-routed file gets its OWN token, bound to that exact file (audit #17),
* so a token cannot be replayed against a different file on the same assembly.
*
* @param array $adapter - Adapter configuration (may contain nested arrays)
* @param string $organism - Organism (token context)
* @param string $assembly - Assembly (token context)
* @param string $track_access_level - Track's access level (for validation warnings)
* @return array - Adapter config with per-file tokens added appropriately
*/
functions.returnDescription: Adapter config with per-file tokens added appropriately

functions.name: moop_stream_file_range
functions.comment:
/**
* Stream $length bytes of $path starting at $start, without ever holding more than one
* chunk in memory.
*
* Two separate memory hazards were being fixed here, both fatal above memory_limit (128M):
*
*  1. php.ini sets `output_buffering = 4096`, so under php-fpm EVERY request begins inside
*     an implicit output buffer that nothing in this file had closed. `readfile()` and
*     `echo` write into whatever buffer is open, so the response accumulated in memory
*     before a byte reached the client. Same root cause as the genome-download 500 fixed in
*     `lib/fasta_download_handler.php` (30ad553); `api/download_file.php` already did the
*     right thing at its :130. This file simply never got the pattern.
*  2. `echo fread($fp, $length)` read the ENTIRE requested range into a PHP string first.
*     An open-ended `Range: bytes=0-` sets $end = filesize-1, which JBrowse does send, so
*     "partial content" could mean the whole BAM. The range path was therefore no safer
*     than the full-file path, which is easy to miss because the name says otherwise.
*
* ob_end_clean() rather than ob_end_flush(): nothing legitimate is in that buffer at this
* point, and flushing stray bytes ahead of binary track data would corrupt it. header()
* queues headers independently of the output buffer, so those are unaffected.
*
* Track files are BAM/bigWig and are large by nature — this endpoint is the one place in
* MOOP where a multi-GB body is the normal case, not the edge case.
*/

functions.name: getContentTypeFromFile
functions.code:
function getContentTypeFromFile($filename) {
    $ext = strtolower(pathinfo($filename, PATHINFO_EXTENSION));
    
    $mime_types = [
        'bw' => 'application/octet-stream',
        'bigwig' => 'application/octet-stream',
        'bam' => 'application/octet-stream',
        'bai' => 'application/octet-stream',
        'cram' => 'application/octet-stream',
        'crai' => 'application/octet-stream',
        'vcf' => 'text/plain',
        'gz' => 'application/gzip',
        'tbi' => 'application/octet-stream',
        'tai' => 'application/octet-stream',  // TAF index files
        'gzi' => 'application/octet-stream',
        'maf' => 'text/plain',
        'bed' => 'text/plain',
        'gff' => 'text/plain',
        'gff3' => 'text/plain',
        'gtf' => 'text/plain',
        'fasta' => 'text/plain',   // data/genomes (genome_file.php)
        'fa' => 'text/plain',
        'fai' => 'text/plain',
        'ix' => 'text/plain',      // trix text-search index
        'ixx' => 'text/plain',
        'json' => 'application/json'
    ];
    
    return $mime_types[$ext] ?? 'application/octet-stream';
}

functions.name: moop_viewing_as_public

/**
* "View as PUBLIC" — an admin's only way to see what an unauthenticated visitor sees.
*
* WHY THIS EXISTS: auto_login_ip_ranges runs below on EVERY request, and logout.php only
* calls session_destroy() — so from inside a trusted subnet you are re-logged-in as
* IP_IN_RANGE on the very next request. There is no way to be logged out from an internal
* address, which means the PUBLIC path (what a visitor actually sees) is otherwise
* impossible to test on a deployment reached only from trusted IPs. Publishing a gene set
* without being able to verify it is publishing blind.
*
* HOW IT WORKS: the real identity stays in $_SESSION untouched; only the ACCESSORS below
* lie. That is what lets view_as.php verify "are you really an admin?" while the rest of
* the app sees a public visitor — an admin can always get back out.
*
* Toggled only via /view_as.php (POST + CSRF + real-admin check).
*/

functions.name: moop_score_config_file
functions.comment:
/**
* What an annotation's Score means, and how to show it.
*
* WHY THIS EXISTS
*
* feature_annotation.score holds many kinds of number under one column heading: E-values
* (lower is better), profile match scores (higher is better), a SignalP probability, a count
* of membrane segments, OMA's relationship as a CODE (1 = 1:1 ... 4 = many:many), the
* closest-gene TIER (1-7), the number of species sharing a duplication. Several kinds sit in
* the same table — the Orthologs table puts "4" (many:many) beside "2e-16" (EggNOG) — so no
* note above a table can explain its column: the meaning changes row by row.
*
* So the meaning travels with the cell. Each source maps to ONE kind; the table formats every
* score from it (words where the number is a code), puts one plain sentence on hover, and
* lists the kinds present in the table's (i) block.
*
* THE LOOKUP TABLE IS EDITABLE: metadata/annotation_scores.json, edited on Admin > Manage
* Annotations ("Score meanings"), so a new analysis needs no code change (user, 2026-10-06).
* The shipped default is metadata/annotation_scores.json.example; it is read until the admin
* first saves. What stays in code is only HOW each display style formats a number.
*
*   kinds: { id: { label, display, explanation, [unit, unit_plural], [words: {"1": "1:1"}] } }
*   rules: [ { [source], [type], kind } ]   `source` matches the START of the source name,
*          `type` the whole annotation type, both case-insensitive; a rule naming both needs both.
*          Two tiers: rules WITH a source are checked first, in file order, first match wins;
*          rules with only a type are FALLBACKS ("anything else in Domains is an E-value"),
*          checked only after every source rule. A fallback therefore can never shadow a
*          specific rule, wherever it sits in the file — when it was one ordered list, moving
*          "Domains -> E-value" above "ProSiteProfiles -> profile score" would have silently
*          made every ProSite score read as an E-value.
*
* Where each default kind comes from in the pipeline (config/build_and_load_db/analysis_parsers/):
*   E-values: DIAMOND, MMseqs2, EggNOG, InterProScan member databases; profile scores:
*   InterProScan ProSiteProfiles/Hamap (column 9); SignalP SP(Sec/SPI) probability; ProtNLM
*   prediction score; DeepTMHMM segment count; OMA relationship (OmaHogOrthologs.pm
*   %RELATIONSHIP_SCORE); OMA paralogs' species count; closest-gene tier/rank
*   (assign_gene_names_v2.pl header).
*
* A source no rule matches keeps the raw number — and is listed on the admin page, so a new
* analysis is noticed rather than silently shown as a bare number.
*/

/** The display styles a kind can use. Code, not data: each one is a formatting rule. */
const MOOP_SCORE_DISPLAYS = [
'evalue'  => 'E-value (short scientific: 2.7e-5)',
'number'  => 'Number (one decimal)',
'percent' => 'Percent (0–1 shown as 0–100%)',
'count'   => 'Count with a unit (7 segments)',
'words'   => 'Words for codes (1 → 1:1)',
'none'    => 'No score (—)',
];

/** The score lookup table: the admin's file, else the shipped default. */

functions.name: blast_failure_for_display
functions.comment:
/**
* What a failed BLAST run may tell the visitor, and whether the failure belongs in the error log.
*
* BLAST's stderr mixes two kinds of failure. Some are the visitor's own input -- BLAST labels
* those "BLAST query/options error:" (e.g. gap costs the chosen matrix does not support) --
* and the visitor needs the message to fix it. Everything else is the server's fault (a
* missing database, a missing binary, a crash), and that text can carry full server paths
* ("No alias or index file found for protein database [/var/www/html/moop/organisms/...]"),
* which a visitor can do nothing with. A reviewer flagged it shown to everyone (2026-11-09).
*
* How much that leak was worth to an attacker, so nobody over- or under-rates it later:
* very little. The path layout (/var/www/html/moop/organisms/{organism}/{assembly}/...) is
* the documented default in the public repository, so it tells an attacker nothing they
* could not read on GitHub. The path also only names the database the visitor picked, and
* tools/blast.php checks assembly access BEFORE running BLAST, so a restricted organism or
* assembly can never surface this way. And knowing a path grants nothing: organism data
* is served through access-checked endpoints, the web server refuses to execute PHP in the
* writable trees (CLAUDE.md §11), and users.json lives outside the document root. What
* the leak could reveal is host detail that is NOT in the repo -- a custom data path, a
* BLAST install location, a temp directory (BLAST names its search path), the BLAST
* version's wording. Low severity, but that, plus "a visitor cannot act on it", is why it
* is hidden rather than left.
*
* So: input errors are shown as BLAST wrote them; server errors get a generic message, are
* logged in full, and only an admin sees the detail on the page. An input-labelled message
* that nonetheless contains an absolute path is treated as a server error -- the label is
* BLAST's, the guarantee about paths is ours.
*
* @param array $result   executeBlastSearch()'s result (uses 'error' and 'stderr')
* @param bool  $is_admin whether the viewer may see server detail
* @return array ['message' => string to show, 'log' => bool (server-side fault)]
*/

parameters.name: is_admin
parameters.description: whether the viewer may see server detail

usages.context: $_f = blast_failure_for_display(['error' => 'BLAST execution failed with code 1', 'stderr' => $_gap], false);
$_f = blast_failure_for_display(['error' => 'x', 'stderr' => 'BLAST query/options error: cannot read [/var/www/q.fa]'], false);
$_f = blast_failure_for_display(['error' => 'The BLAST queue is full', 'stderr' => ''], false);

functions.name: blast_job_formats
functions.comment:
/**
* BLAST results saved on the server, and BLAST jobs run in the background (api/v1/blast.php).
*
* ONE place for a finished search's files. The BLAST page and the API both save the three
* downloads here and both serve them through api/blast_download.php, so what an agent hands a
* person is byte for byte what that person gets from the page (Sofia's rule, 2026-11-24).
* Until then the page put the text in hidden <div>s and the browser posted it back to be
* echoed: the TXT gained 29 leading characters of template indentation and all three came
* back with Windows (CRLF) line endings, because a form submission converts line breaks --
* a hidden "\r" on the TSV's last column.
*
*   {cache}/blast_jobs/<id>/            one folder per search; <id> = 32 random hex (the only key)
*       request.json    API jobs: what to run (database path resolved and access-checked by
*                       the web request; this folder is never served)
*       worker.lock     held (flock) by the background worker for as long as it lives
*       blast_results.{txt,tsv,xml}     the downloads, exactly as blast_formatter wrote them
*       result.json     written LAST, atomically: state done|failed (+ message)
*
* Built like blast_queue.php so a job cannot get stuck: no "running" flag is ever stored.
* A job is finished when result.json exists; alive while worker.lock is held; and if neither,
* past a short start-up grace, the worker died -- the kernel dropped its lock -- and the job
* reads "failed". Folders are swept after BLAST_JOB_KEEP_SECONDS by housekeeping.
*
* Anyone holding the id can fetch the files (that is what lets an agent hand a link to a
* person). The id is 128 random bits, and the results only ever contain databases the
* submitter could open.
*/

require_once __DIR__ . '/cache_paths.php';
require_once __DIR__ . '/functions_system.php';

const BLAST_JOB_KEEP_SECONDS  = 86400;   // files kept 24 h
const BLAST_JOB_START_GRACE   = 30;      // seconds a just-spawned worker has to take its lock

/** Download format => [file name in the job folder, MIME type, key in runBlastSearch()'s result]. */

blast_queue_dir
functions.comment:
/**
* BLAST queue: at most a memory budget's worth of BLAST runs at once; the rest wait in line.
*
* Why: the capacity test (notes/CAPACITY_TEST_2026-10-23.md) found that nothing limited
* concurrent BLASTs, and a genome tblastn needs 1.2 GB (bat) to 2.9 GB (wallaby). Eight at
* once ran the 15 GB server out of memory and took the site down.
*
* Built so that it CANNOT get stuck. There is no job table, no worker process and no
* "running" flag to go stale -- the failure that plagues queue-table designs (a job marked
* running forever after its worker died). Every piece of state is a flock() held by the PHP
* request that owns it, and the kernel releases a flock the instant its process dies, however
* it dies (OOM kill, crash, php-fpm restart). A leftover FILE means nothing; only a held LOCK
* counts, and dead files are swept by whoever sees them.
*
*   {cache}/blast_queue/units/u00..   one file per memory unit (BLAST_QUEUE_UNIT_MB). A running
*                                     search holds as many unit locks as it is estimated to need.
*   {cache}/blast_queue/wait/<seq>-<ticket>   held by each waiting request; sorted by seq it is
*                                     the line. Only the head of the line tries to start, so a
*                                     big search cannot be starved by a stream of small ones.
*   {cache}/blast_queue/run/<ticket>  held while a search runs; counted for the status line.
*
* Bounded both ways: a request waits at most blast_queue_max_wait seconds, then gives up with
* a "busy, try again" message; a running BLAST is killed after blast_max_runtime seconds
* (`timeout`, see blast_queue_wrap_command()), so a runaway cannot hold its units forever.
*
* Fails OPEN: if the queue directory cannot be used, the search runs unqueued and the reason
* goes to the error log -- a broken queue must never stop BLAST.
*/

require_once __DIR__ . '/cache_paths.php';
require_once __DIR__ . '/functions_system.php';

const BLAST_QUEUE_UNIT_MB = 256;

/** The queue directory, or '' if it cannot be created. */

functions.comment:

*   blast_max_concurrent    searches running at once, whatever their size. More than
*                           cores/threads only makes every search slower, not more of them
*                           finish (measured: flat to 4 on 8 cores x 2 threads, then linear).
*   blast_queue_max_wait    seconds a request waits for its turn before giving up.
*   blast_max_runtime       seconds a single BLAST may run before it is killed.
*
* max_wait + max_runtime must stay under nginx's fastcgi_read_timeout for the BLAST pages,
* or nginx gives the user a 504 while the search carries on without them.
*/

usages.context: return 'This search ran longer than the ' . blast_queue_settings()['max_runtime']

functions.name: moop_ensure_cache_dir
functions.comment:
/**
* Create a cache directory if it does not exist.
*
* Returns false rather than throwing: a cache we cannot write is a performance
* problem, never a correctness one, so every caller is expected to carry on
* without caching rather than fail the request.
*
* The chmod after mkdir is NOT redundant. mkdir()'s mode argument is masked by the
* process umask, so `mkdir($dir, 0775)` under the usual umask 022 produces 0755 — group
* readable, group NOT writable. When a CLI script (running as the owner) creates the
* directory first, php-fpm can then never write into it.
*
* That is not hypothetical: on 2026-08-03, 281 of 282 directories under cache_path were
* 2750, so php-fpm could not write a single cache file. Nothing errored, because callers
* fall back to computing the value live and ignore the failed write — which meant 95 of
* 96 gene sets re-ran getAnnotatedFeatureTypesInGeneSet() on EVERY gene page load, at
* 349ms cold each time. A cache that cannot be written is invisible by construction, so
* the mode has to be forced at creation. lib/permission_check.php now also sweeps this
* tree, because the same drift can arrive from outside this function.
*/

* assuming 'mRNA' is wrong for 6 of 85 databases in a way that fails silently. Measured

functions.name: moop_organism_cache_refresh_active
functions.comment:
/**
* Is a background organism-cache refresh actually running right now?
*
* THE ONE definition of "refreshing". Three callers used to answer this question
* separately -- admin/api/refresh_organism_cache.php (PID liveness), lib/housekeeping.php
* (PID liveness) and admin/pages/admin.php via admin/admin.php (lock exists AND mtime
* < 600s). The dashboard's mtime variant is what wedged the UI on 2026-08-04: a refresh
* completed at 08:17:32 but its background shell never reached the `rm -f` that drops the
* lock, so the lock sat there holding a fresh mtime. The dashboard read that as "in
* progress" and rendered the spinner; the status endpoint read the same lock, saw the PID
* was dead, reported `idle` and the JS jumped the bar to 100%. Banner and bar disagreed
* until a poll happened to unlink the lock. Two answers to one question, so one of them
* was always going to be wrong.
*
* mtime cannot answer this. It says when the lock was CREATED, not whether the worker
* lives -- an orphan under 600s reads as running, and a genuine scan past 600s reads as
* finished. The PID does answer it, so that is the only check here.
*
* Side effect by design: a lock whose process is gone is REMOVED. That is what makes the
* wedge self-healing rather than something an admin has to clear by hand -- whichever
* caller notices first cleans up for everyone.
*/

/**
* Content pages: pages an admin writes in Markdown (About, Protocols, FAQ, ...) -- cuttingclass
* step 2 (notes/CUTTINGCLASS_PLAN.md). Opt-in: a site with no pages shows nothing new, and a page
* appears in a menu only when a menu links it.
*
* Each page is one file, {metadata_path}/pages/{slug}.json -- SITE DATA, not code, so the
* housekeeping snapshot copies it into the private site-data repo:
*
*   { "slug": "about-simrbase",
*     "title": {"en": "About SIMRbase", "es": "Acerca de SIMRbase"},
*     "body":  {"en": "# ...markdown...", "es": "..."},
*     "updated_at": "2026-11-03T16:40:00-06:00", "updated_by": "admin" }
*
* Languages are the site's (Admin -> Manage Languages, ConfigManager::languages()). A page keeps
* the text of EVERY language it was written in, retired ones included: retiring a language hides
* it, it never deletes what was written (the retired-organism rule), and saving a page in the
* editor -- which only shows the active languages -- leaves the others untouched. Until the
* language work (step 5) chooses per visitor, a page is shown in English.
*
* A page is written in Markdown (the default) or HTML ('format'), the same for every language.
* ONE renderer -- moop_page_render() -- for the published page, the home AND the editor's preview
* (admin/api/preview_page.php), so the preview can never disagree with what visitors see:
*   markdown  Parsedown in SAFE MODE: typed HTML is shown as text, javascript: links neutralised.
*   html      written as-is (cards, grids, Bootstrap classes), then cleaned by HTML Purifier --
*             a maintained sanitiser, not ours: scripts, on*= handlers, javascript: links, iframes
*             and forms are removed; class and style are kept. The site's CSP still allows inline
*             script, so this cleaning is what stops a page from carrying one.
*/

require_once __DIR__ . '/access_rules.php';

functions.name: moop_crawler_claimed
functions.comment:
/**
* Is this request really from Google's, Bing's or DuckDuckGo's search crawler?
*
* Why: the human check (lib/human_check.php) turned every search engine away along with the
* scrapers, so no page of the site could appear in search results (seen 2026-11-23). A search
* crawler cannot solve a challenge, but it CAN be proven genuine, the way each engine documents:
*   - Google, Bing: reverse DNS of the address ends in their domain, AND that name resolves back
*     to the same address (a scraper can set any User-Agent, and can even control its own reverse
*     DNS, but not Google's forward DNS).
*   - DuckDuckGo: the address is in its published list (duckduckbot.json, refreshed weekly by
*     housekeeping task crawler_lists). DuckDuckGo publishes no reverse-DNS names.
* Anything merely CLAIMING to be one of them in its User-Agent is checked; nothing else is, so
* ordinary visitors never cost a DNS lookup. Results are cached per address for a day (both yes
* and no), so each address costs at most one lookup a day.
*
* A verified crawler is let past the human check for PAGES only (human_check.php) -- never the
* API, AJAX, downloads or exports -- and robots.txt still decides which pages it should fetch.
*/

require_once __DIR__ . '/cache_paths.php';

const MOOP_CRAWLER_CACHE_TTL = 86400;
const MOOP_CRAWLER_DDG_URL   = 'https://duckduckgo.com/duckduckbot.json';

/** Which crawler the User-Agent claims to be: 'google' | 'bing' | 'duckduckgo' | null. */

functions.name: moop_search_input_is_usable
functions.comment:
/**
* Is this search input worth running? Mirrors js/modules/search-terms.js.
*
* THE RULE: at least one term of 2+ characters. Per-term, NOT total input length.
*
* Terms are AND-ed into a prefix query below, so a short term alongside others is
* constrained by them; a short term alone is not. Measured on Myotis_myotis:
*
*   "1"*                                      1,855,918 rows   <- alone: useless
*   "histone"* AND "deacetylase"*                 9,258 rows
*   "histone"* AND "deacetylase"* AND "1"*        4,254 rows   <- keeping it HELPS
*
* So short terms are kept, not dropped -- dropping them was costing precision. What must
* be refused is a query with nothing selective in it at all: `a` matches 1,164,973 rows
* against a 2,500 cap, so the user gets 2,500 arbitrary rows.
*
* The previous gate tested total length >= 3 in TWO JavaScript files and nothing here.
* That blocked real two-character gene symbols outright -- AR, C3, F8 (haemophilia A), CS,
* PC, SI -- with no search run and no explanation, while `histone deacetylase 1` passed
* only because the whole string is long.
*
* This copy is the load-bearing one. The JS gives a fast, specific message, but a
* hand-made request bypasses it entirely, and a lone `1` fanned out across selected
* organisms is a 1.86M-row scan per database against a 32 ms disk.
*/

usages.context: ok(moop_search_input_is_usable('AR', false), 'a two-letter gene symbol is searchable (AR, C3, F8)');
ok(!moop_search_input_is_usable('a', false), 'a single letter is refused, not run against every record');

functions.name: moop_porter_stem
functions.comment:
/**
* The porter stem of one term, as SQLite's OWN tokenizer computes it.
*
* Asked of SQLite rather than reimplemented in PHP on purpose: the stem has to agree with
* what the index actually stored, and a hand-written porter would have to be kept in sync
* with SQLite's forever (js/modules/search-terms.js declines the same job for the same
* reason). An in-memory database, so it touches no organism file and needs no write access.
*
* Returns '' when the term is not a single word, when stemming is unavailable, or when the
* stem is not a prefix of the term. Every caller treats '' as "skip the stem tier", so a
* failure here degrades to the previous ranking rather than breaking search.
*
* THE PREFIX GUARANTEE. SQLite's porter only ever TRUNCATES -- verified against the
* tokenizer across the suffix-replacing cases the textbook algorithm rewrites:
*
*   relational -> relat   (not "relate")     electricity -> electr
*   digitizer  -> digit                      vietnamization -> vietnam
*   transposases -> transposas               transposons -> transposon
*
* so the stem is always a leading substring of the typed word. The check below enforces
* that rather than trusting it, because the whole point of the stem tier is that
* '%stem%' is a LOOSER pattern than '%term%' -- if some future tokenizer returned a stem
* that were not a prefix, the tier would silently rank on an unrelated string.
*/

functions.name: ftsStemLikePattern
functions.comment:
/**
* The LIKE pattern for the stem-match ranking tier, or '' when that tier does not apply.
*
* WHY THIS TIER EXISTS. FTS5 matched on the stem, but the literal tier above it tests the
* word the user TYPED, so a plural search credits only the rows carrying that same plural
* -- and in this data the singular is far more common. Measured on
* Craseonycteris_thonglongyai, "transposons": 234 matching rows, of which just 2 contain
* "transposons" but 125 contain "transposon". Two rows therefore decided the whole top of
* the list and everything below them fell back to bm25, which put six annotations of one
* unnamed gene -- "Homeodomain-like", "consensus disorder prediction", "-" -- above MAEL,
* whose description reads "maelstrom spermatogenic transposon silencer". Same shape for
* "transposases" (27 of 517 -> 336) and "receptors" (7,155 of 146,173 -> 57,673).
*
* WHY IT IS ADDED BENEATH THE LITERAL TIER RATHER THAN REPLACING IT. The literal tier is
* load-bearing: it is what fixed the porter precision bug, where "transpos" stems to
* "transpo" and so prefix-matches TRANSPORT. Widening that tier to the stem would hand
* that back. Keeping the exact tier first cannot: for "transpos" the 1,326 rows containing
* it still sort above the 64,725 the stem reaches, so the top 100 is untouched --
* confirmed 100/100 relevant before and after. "kinase" is unaffected by construction
* (36,434 rows match '%kinase%' and '%kinas%' alike).
*
* Quoted phrases are deliberately excluded: a phrase has no single stem, and phrase search
* is the tool a user reaches for when they want exactness.
*/

functions.comment:

* Execute a prepared FTS search and apply the shared row cap + warning.
*
* The SQL is expected to SELECT one extra row than the cap (moop_search_query_limit())
* so we can detect "more results exist". Unlike the old LIKE path, DB errors are
* surfaced (and logged) instead of being silently swallowed — a missing FTS index (an
* organism.sqlite built without build_fts_index.sql) is reported clearly rather
* than crashing the whole cross-organism search.
*/

functions.name: moop_id_match_ladder
functions.comment:
/**
* The version-tolerance ladder for matching a user-supplied feature ID.
*
* Returns the match attempts IN ORDER, each as ['op' => '=' | 'GLOB', 'val' => …]. Callers
* run them until one produces rows; exact-as-typed is always first, so an ID that genuinely
* exists as typed is never shadowed by a versioned near-match.
*
* Extracted 2026-08-05 because a THIRD surface needed it. MOOP displays versioned accessions
* (NV2t021704001.1) while users paste IDs from papers, spreadsheets and older releases where
* the version is absent or stale. Each surface that got this wrong failed differently and
* silently: the index box said "no results", and MOOPmart's By-Feature-IDs resolved nothing
* and exported an empty file with no explanation.
*
* ⚠️ GLOB, never LIKE. Both express "starts with", but SQLite's LIKE is case-insensitive by
* default and therefore cannot use the BINARY-collated feature_uniquename index — it
* degrades to a full scan, which matters enormously on an endpoint that fans out across
* every accessible database. GLOB is case-sensitive and keeps the index seek.
*
* @param string $q The ID as the user typed it.
* @return array<int, array{op:string, val:string}>
*/

parameters.name: q
parameters.description: The ID as the user typed it.

functions.name: moop_resolve_input_ids
functions.comment:
/**
* Resolve user-typed feature IDs to the uniquenames that actually exist in ONE database.
*
* Version-tolerant via moop_id_match_ladder(). Returns [input_id => [uniquename, …]] for
* everything that resolved, and fills $unresolved with the inputs that matched nothing.
*
* ⚠️ AMBIGUITY IS REPORTED, NOT RESOLVED. If "X" matches both X.1 and X.2 the caller gets
* BOTH (user decision, 2026-08-05: "list both, export both, report it"). Silently picking
* one would mean an export whose contents depend on a tie-break nobody can see.
*
* ⚠️ The unresolved list is the point, not a nicety. Before this, an unmatched ID was simply
* absent from the result, so pasting 50 IDs of which 3 were stale produced a smaller export
* and said nothing — the "a miss deletes, silently" shape this codebase keeps hitting.
*/

functions.name: moop_annotation_levels
functions.comment:
/**
* The feature levels that actually carry annotations in ONE database.
*
* Returns e.g. ['mRNA'], or ['gene'] for Bradyrhizobium, or ['transcript'] for the two
* Schmidtea that use it. Falls back to ['mRNA'] only when the query cannot run at all.
*
* ⚠️ DO NOT replace this with the literal 'mRNA'. That is the whole point of the function.
* Measured across all 85 databases 2026-08-05:
*     mRNA        2,980,598 annotated features   79 organisms
*     transcript     48,562                       2 organisms
*     gene            7,812                       9 organisms (7,708 = Bradyrhizobium)
* A hardcoded 'mRNA' silently returns ZERO annotation results for Bradyrhizobium — a
* bacterium, whose annotations are gene-level by nature — and drops 48,562 rows across the
* two Schmidtea. Correct for 79 of 85 is not correct.
*
* The 1% cutoff drops noise rather than structure: Petromyzon_marinus carries 83,343
* mRNA-level annotations and 13 stray gene-level ones. Those 13 are a data artifact, and
* admitting 'gene' on their account would re-introduce the gene+mRNA duplication for that
* organism's entire name search. A level has to be genuinely used to count.
*
* See notes/SEARCH_FEATURE_LEVEL_DECISION.md.
*
* @return string[] Non-empty list of feature_type values.
*/

functions.name: searchFeaturesByNameDescription
functions.comment:
/**
* Search features by name and description only (gene-centric) — no annotation join.
* Used when the user has explicitly deselected all annotation sources. Backed by the
* feature_search FTS index, which covers EVERY feature (including unannotated ones).
* Returns rows in the same column shape as searchFeaturesAndAnnotations (annotation
* columns NULL) so the result-formatting code in the AJAX endpoint is unchanged.
*/

functions.name: moop_interleave_by_source
functions.comment:
/**
* Stop one annotation source from owning the first screen. REORDERS, never drops.
*
* The quota pool balances annotation TYPES, which is the curated concept -- but a user
* sees SOURCES, and one type can be served by very few of them. Gene Ontology is a single
* type fed mainly by EggNOG2GO and InterPro2GO, so giving it a fair type share handed it a
* larger source share than bm25 did: measured on Rhinolophus, "binding" went from 37 of
* the top 100 from its biggest source to 56, and "ubiquitin" 20 to 27. Better on types,
* worse on the thing displayed.
*
* So: take the first $cap rows of each source, then the next $cap of each, and so on.
* Rank order is preserved WITHIN each block, and every row is kept -- rows past the cap
* move down the list, they do not disappear. With ~7-24 sources and a cap of 25, block
* zero alone covers far more than one screen.
*/

functions.name: moop_fts_type_code
functions.comment:
/**
* The FTS token identifying one annotation type inside feature_annotation_search.
*
* MUST mirror the expression in build_fts_index.sql exactly, or the pool silently
* selects nothing for that type and its quota is lost. strtolower(), not mb_strtolower():
* SQLite's lower() is ASCII-only, and a type with a non-ASCII capital must produce the
* same token on both sides. Separators are stripped rather than replaced because
* unicode61 splits on '_' and porter then stems the pieces -- "RBBH_Homolog" and
* "Homologs" both index "homolog", which made the Homologs filter return 870,674 rows
* where 69,398 qualify. One token per type has no shared stem with any other.
*/

functions.name: moop_fts_has_type_column
functions.comment:
/**
* Does this organism's index carry annotation_type_code (i.e. has it been rebuilt)?
*
* Quota pooling needs that column. Databases indexed before it existed must keep working
* unchanged, so every caller falls back to the bm25 pool when this is false -- which is
* what makes the re-index a rolling operation rather than a flag day.
*/

functions.name: moop_types_with_annotations
functions.comment:

* Narrow the types a database declares to those the sources cache says have annotations.

* Fails toward searching MORE, never less: if the cache names none of the declared types

* than leaving search with no types at all.
*
* @param array $present      [type => true] from annotation_source
* @param array $cached_types type names that have annotations, per the cache
* @return array [type => true]
*/

functions.name: moop_resolve_hits_to_level
functions.comment:
/**
* Collapse ID-search hits onto ONE level per gene, by RESOLVING rather than filtering.
*
* An ID search returns several rows for one gene whenever the child IDs happen to nest inside
* the parent's, and `LIKE '%term%'` then matches all of them. "NV2t021704001" returns 3 rows.
*
* ⚠️ That nesting is NOT a universal MOOP rule, and assuming it is would be wrong. Depositor
* IDs are preserved (see [[feedback_original_data_stays_original]]); `…:cds`/`…:pep` is
* specifically the transcript2gene path suffixing MOOP's OWN copies to disambiguate them.
* Other sources nest differently or not at all:
*     T2G      NV2t021704001.1        :cds / :pep   -> children CONTAIN the parent id
*     RefSeq   WP_011083461.1         cds-…         -> child contains it via a PREFIX
*     Ensembl  FBtr0070000 / FBpp…    independent   -> no nesting, no duplication at all
* Which is exactly why this resolves through the hierarchy rather than pattern-matching
* IDs: a string rule that fits one convention silently misses the others.
*
* ⚠️ FILTERING (what the name/description path does) IS WRONG HERE. Dropping every row that
* is not at the annotation-bearing level means a user pasting a protein accession
* (`…​.1:pep`) gets NOTHING — a gene that exists reported as missing. That is a worse and
* quieter failure than the duplication. So a child hit is replaced by its parent instead of
* being discarded, and the row that survives carries `matched_uniquename` so the UI can say
* "matched …:pep" rather than silently showing an ID the user never typed.
*
* ⚠️ BOUNDED WALK, never an unbounded recursive one. `parent_feature_id` has held self-loops
* in the wild — Schmidtea_lugubris carried 14,313 before its 2026-08-05 reload, and the other
* databases are not reloaded yet. An unbounded walk pins a php-fpm worker (SQLite 3.34.1 here
* has no CYCLE clause). This climbs at most MOOP_RESOLVE_MAX_DEPTH levels, in batched
* queries, and stops early when nothing moved.
*
* ⚠️ A SINGLE step is NOT enough, which is easy to assume and wrong. The chain is
* mRNA → cds → protein: `:cds` hangs off the transcript but `:pep` hangs off the CDS, so a
* protein is TWO steps from the annotation-bearing level. Resolving one step turned a
* protein hit into a CDS hit and the duplicate simply reappeared one row down.
*
* ⚠️ NEVER DROPS A ROW. A hit whose parent cannot be resolved — missing, self-referential,
* or one of the 'NULL'/'' text values the old loaders wrote — is kept exactly as it was.
* Losing a result to a failed lookup is the "a miss deletes" shape that has bitten this
* codebase before.
*
* See notes/SEARCH_FEATURE_LEVEL_DECISION.md.
*/

functions.name: moop_drop_hits_whose_child_is_shown
functions.comment:
/**
* One row for a gene and its own transcript when both matched -- both open the same gene page.
* WHICH row: the one whose ID is exactly what was typed (case ignored); if neither, the
* transcript (the annotation level). So typing a gene ID shows the gene: dd_Smed_v6_2529_0
* would otherwise show only its mRNA dd_Smed_v6_2529_0_1, which also matched. 2026-11-19, Sofia: the group page listed SMED30003001 (transcript) AND
* gene-SMED30003001 (gene) for one ID, while the menu-bar box gave one result. The gene's id
* contains the transcript's, so both match; a gene cannot be lifted DOWN, so the climb above
* kept both (notes/SEARCH_FEATURE_LEVEL_DECISION.md, "Petromyzon keeps 2 by design" -- reversed).
*
* Never loses a gene: a gene whose children did NOT match stays. Direct children only (gene ->
* mRNA, the shape every gene set here has). Rows without feature_id/parent_feature_id are kept.
*/

functions.name: getAnnotationSourcesByGeneSet
functions.comment:
/**
* Per GENE SET, per source: how many GENES carry it (and how many distinct terms it has).
*
* Genes, not terms, since 2026-10-22. The old count was distinct annotations, so a filter
* offered "InterProScan (Coils) (1)" while 13,090 Nematostella proteins have a coiled coil:
* one term, "Coil". Someone choosing a filter wants to know how much of the gene set it
* reaches. A gene also belongs to exactly one gene set, so gene counts add up across gene
* sets and organisms -- the term counts did not (a term shared by two gene sets counted twice).
*
* "Gene" = the feature's root: annotations sit on transcripts (sometimes genes, or proteins),
* so a feature is traced up at most two parents. In a gene set with no gene models the root
* is the transcript, so there the number counts transcripts. Self-parents are skipped, as a
* few databases had them (see the feature table DDL).
*
* The per-TYPE total is a separate distinct count: one gene with both Pfam and InterPro is
* two source hits but one Domains gene, so summing the sources would overstate it.
*
* EXPENSIVE: two walks of feature_annotation, ~8 s each warm on Nematostella (5.1 M links),
* so it is never run in a page request -- housekeeping builds it in the background run, once
* per database change (moop_gene_set_annotation_counts_file()).
*
* Keyed "{assembly accession}/{gene set name}": a gene set name is unique per assembly, not
* per organism (gene_set UNIQUE(genome_id, gene_set_name)), so the name alone could merge two.
*
* @return array  ['sources' => {"acc/gs": {type: [{name, count, terms}, ...]}},
*                 'type_genes' => {"acc/gs": {type: genes}}]; empty arrays on error.
*/

* annotation_config.json's annotation_type_order gives, then any others. Shared by the
* organism-wide and per-gene-set counts so the two can never be ordered differently.
*/

* Parse the feature IDs a user typed, each optionally followed by a range.

* Entries are separated by newlines or commas. A range is the trailing part of an entry:

functions.name: expandFeaturesToAllSequenceTypes
functions.comment:
/**
* Expand selected features to every related feature that has a sequence.
*
* extractSequencesForAllTypes() buckets each id by ITS OWN feature_type, so handing it a
* list of mRNAs yields mRNA sequences and nothing else. The search-results FASTA button
* did exactly that, which is why it returned only transcripts while the gene page and
* Retrieve Sequences return all three.
*
* ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
* DELIBERATELY FEATURE-TYPE AGNOSTIC
*
* This walks the parent/child graph and never names a feature type. The rule is simply:
*
*     take every ANCESTOR and every DESCENDANT of what the user selected.
*
* On today's gene -> mRNA -> CDS -> protein hierarchy that produces exactly the right
* answer, and it keeps producing it if the hierarchy ever changes shape:
*
*   selected a gene     -> descendants = all isoforms and their CDS/proteins
*   selected one mRNA   -> descendants = that isoform's CDS/protein; ancestors = its gene
*   selected a protein  -> ancestors  = its CDS, mRNA and gene
*
* Note what this does NOT do: it never takes the descendants OF an ancestor. That is what
* keeps a single selected isoform from dragging in its sibling isoforms, and it falls out
* of the shape of the walk rather than from a special case.
*
* Types that have no per-feature FASTA (gene, exon, ...) cost nothing to include —
* extractSequencesForAllTypes() drops them via _fasta_key_for_type(). So this function
* does not need to know which types those are either.
*
* Scoped by assembly / gene set when given: a feature_uniquename is unique only within a
* gene set (see buildTypedIds()). The walk itself stays inside one gene set naturally,
* because parent and child rows share a gene_set_id.
*

*                             the family the header context is worked out from

* @return array uniquename => feature_type, ready for extractSequencesForAllTypes()
*/

parameters.name: gene_set_ids

parameters.name: family
parameters.description: optional, filled with every row both walks returned, feature_id =>

* the document root. Messages may carry an email address, so they are treated like credentials:
* 0640, never world-readable, a 'sensitive' permission rule (lib/permission_check.php), and copied to
* the private site-data backup by housekeeping_snapshot_site_data(). The folder is already labelled

* never leaves half a file -- and moop_feedback_add() REPORTS failure; the form never says "sent"
* for a message that was not saved (CLAUDE.md §11: silent write failures).

* per-session limit (5 an hour) and a site-wide cap (MOOP_FEEDBACK_DAY_CAP a day).
*/

const MOOP_FEEDBACK_DAY_CAP = 100;

*
* @return array<string, array{label: string, issue: string}> in checklist order
*/

function moop_organism_check_defs(): array {
    $d = fn($label, $issue) => compact('label', 'issue');
    return [
        'has_assemblies'        => $d('Has assemblies', 'no-assemblies'),
        'has_fasta'             => $d('Has FASTA files', 'no-fasta'),
        'gene_sets_complete'    => $d('Every assembly has a gene set with Protein, mRNA and CDS FASTA', 'gene-set-files'),
        'has_blast_indexes'     => $d('Has BLAST indexes', 'blast'),
        'has_fai_index'         => $d('Has FAI index', 'fai'),
        'seqnames_match_genome' => $d('Gene sets name chromosomes as the genome does', 'seqnames'),
        'has_database'          => $d('Has database file', 'no-database'),
        'database_valid'        => $d('Database is valid', 'db-invalid'),
        'directories_match_db'  => $d('Assembly & gene set dirs match DB', 'dir-mismatch'),
        'assemblies_in_groups'  => $d('Assembly in organism groups', 'groups'),
        'in_taxonomy_tree'      => $d('In taxonomy tree', 'tree'),
        'metadata_complete'     => $d('Metadata complete', 'metadata'),

}

functions.name: moop_organism_severity
functions.comment:
/**
* Grade an organism's overall_status into a severity: 'complete' | 'critical' | 'incomplete'.
*
* WHY THIS EXISTS. Severity used to be derived from how MANY checks passed:
*
*     $all_pass ? 'complete' : ($pass_count > 0 ? 'incomplete' : 'critical')
*
* which made 'critical' unreachable. It required an organism to fail ALL TEN checks --
* simultaneously no assemblies, no FASTA, no database, no metadata, not in the tree --
* which cannot happen for anything that exists on disk. Measured across all 85 organisms
* on 2026-09-17: the minimum pass_count was 9, and 'critical' fired for ZERO of them. So a
* three-state scale was really two, and a database that returns nothing to every user wore
* the same amber "Incomplete" as a missing .fai index.
*
* Count is an arithmetic proxy with no relation to consequence. This grades by IMPACT
* instead -- the same principle CLAUDE.md section 11 applies to filesystem permissions
* ("judge by IMPACT, not an exact mode").
*
* CRITICAL means: the organism is listed, but cannot serve data to a user. Group and
* taxonomy-tree membership are deliberately NOT here -- they are admin configuration an
* organism passes through on its way in, they have their own badges, and they do not mean
* the data is broken.

functions.name: countJBrowseRegistrations
functions.comment:
/**
* Return every JBrowse assembly registration whose source data is gone.
*
* Every other data-health check in this file walks OUTWARD from the organisms tree or the
* database. This one walks the other way — from the derived JBrowse artifacts back to their
* source — because that is the only direction that catches source data being renamed or
* removed OUTSIDE MOOP. Registration builds a data/genomes/{org}/{asm}/ directory holding a
* reference.fasta symlink into organisms/; an admin never creates those by hand and has no
* reason to know they exist, so nothing prompts them to clean up after a rename.
*
* The check is deliberately on the ARTIFACT, not on names: a registration is broken if its
* reference.fasta no longer resolves, whatever the cause (directory renamed, genome.fa
* deleted underneath it, source tree unmounted). A dangling symlink serves HTTP 404 to
* every user who opens that assembly in the genome browser.
*
* Reads ~69 small JSON files + two stat calls each (~2ms), same cost class as the other
* checks here, so it can run on every dashboard / Manage Organisms load.
*
* NOTE: report-only, by design. This must never auto-remove a registration — a temporarily
* absent source (unmounted share, mid-flight rsync, half-finished load) is indistinguishable
* from a deliberate deletion, and acting on it would destroy a working setup.
*
* @param string $organism_data_path Path to organisms directory
* @return array List of ['organism','assembly','reason','detail']
*/

moop_naming_tag_key
functions.comment:
/**
* What each part of a naming tag means -- the ONE copy, read by the help topic
* (tools/pages/help/gene-names.php) and the agent guide (llms.php), so the two cannot drift.
*
* Source: the naming script itself, config/build_and_load_db/analysis_parsers/assign_gene_names_v2.pl
* (sub tagged and its comment block, oma_support(), relationship_tag(), swissprot_name(); compute
* side owns it), with notes/GENE_NAMING_METHODS.md "Evidence tags". Checked against every gene
* description in every organism.sqlite on 2026-11-24: 1.67M tagged genes, none with a code missing
* here. Facts that are easy to get wrong:
*   - sim and pthr are written ONLY by oma_support(), i.e. on names from a human OMA ortholog (ISO);
*     plus sim~ on an ISM name (a partial human homolog). Never on a -like name.
*   - pthr+ compares the gene's own PANTHER family (InterProScan) with the family of the human gene
*     the name comes from (Swiss-Prot) -- not with the gene's top similarity hit.
* If the pipeline adds a code, add it here.
*
* English only, like the methods notes; the help page prints it through t_plain().
*
* @return array{kinds: list<array{0:string,1:string,2:string,3:string,4:string}>,
*               details: list<array{0:string,1:string,2:string}>, support: list<array{0:string,1:string,2:string}>,
*               marks: list<array{0:string,1:string}>}
*         kinds: [code, the words it stands for, short label, meaning, a real example];
*         details/support: [code, the words it stands for ('' when it is a plain word), meaning]
*/
functions.code:
function moop_naming_tag_key(): array
{
    return [
        // The first code: what kind of evidence named the gene. Modelled on the Gene Ontology's
        // evidence codes (ISO, ISS, ISM, TAS are GO codes; SRC is MOOP's own).
        'kinds' => [
            ['TAS', 'Traceable Author Statement', 'Curated',
                'A person chose the name, usually from published work. It is used as given.',
                'Hox2/3a: homeobox 2/3a [TAS]'],
            ['SRC', 'Source', 'From the source',
                'The name came with the gene set (RefSeq, Ensembl or the authors), or from another annotation of '
                . 'the same species. The tag does not judge it: the name is kept as given, even when the gene\'s own '
                . 'evidence (its protein family and domains) points to a different gene, so check that evidence before '
                . 'relying on the name. When a code follows SRC (1to1, rbh, bh), it describes the match to the gene in '
                . 'that other annotation, not to a human gene.',
                'KICSTOR complex protein SZT2 [SRC]'],
            ['ISO', 'Inferred from Sequence Orthology', 'Ortholog',
                'Named from an orthology call (OMA, or the PANTHER tree) to a human gene: the strongest evidence '
                . 'that this is the same gene. The name is the human one, with no "-like" (or, for a family of '
                . 'co-orthologs, the family\'s name).',
                'FANCE: FA complementation group E [ISO|1to1|sim+|pthr+|tree+|hog]'],
            ['ISS', 'Inferred from Sequence Similarity', 'Similar (homolog)',
                'The name ends in "-like": the protein aligns along most of its length to the named protein, '
                . 'human or of another species, but orthology is not shown. It may be a paralog.',
                'PARP14-like: poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase family member 14-like [ISS|rbh]'],
            ['ISM', 'Inferred from Sequence Model', 'Family or domain',
                'The name says "family member" or "domain-containing protein": the evidence stops at a protein '
                . 'family or domain and does not point to one gene.',
                'Reverse transcriptase domain-containing protein [ISM|ipr]'],
        ],
        // What follows: how the call was made.
        'details' => [
            ['1to1', 'one to one', 'After ISO: this gene and the human gene are each other\'s only ortholog. After SRC: '
                . 'this gene and the gene in the other annotation it was named from are the same gene, matched one to '
                . 'one -- it says nothing about a human gene.'],
            ['3to1, 7to1, ...', 'N to one', 'That many genes in this gene set are orthologs of one human gene and '
                . 'share its name, numbered "(1 of 3)".'],
            ['mto1', 'many to one', 'Several genes here are orthologs of one human gene, but only one carries its name.'],
            ['fam', 'family', 'Several genes here and several human genes form one ortholog family; the gene is named '
                . 'for the family.'],
            ['tree', '', 'Orthology from the PANTHER tree, which places the gene with exactly one human gene. Followed '
                . 'by how the closest human gene was found: rbh, via or bh.'],
            ['rbh', 'reciprocal best hit', 'Each protein is the other\'s best match.'],
            ['bh', 'best hit', 'The named protein is this one\'s best match; the match is not reciprocal.'],
            ['via', '', 'Through another species: this gene\'s ortholog there is an ortholog of the human gene.'],
            ['sp', 'Swiss-Prot', 'The match is a reviewed Swiss-Prot protein of another species, named in brackets '
                . 'after the name.'],
            ['tie-rbh', 'tie, reciprocal best hit', 'Human paralogs scored almost the same; the reciprocal best hit decided.'],
            ['tie-grp', 'tie, group', 'Human paralogs scored almost the same; the gene is named for their group.'],
            ['pthr', 'PANTHER', 'Named for a PANTHER protein family.'],
            ['rpt', 'repeat', 'Named for a family defined by a repeated domain.'],
            ['ipr', 'InterPro', 'Named for an InterPro domain.'],
            ['te', 'transposable element', 'A transposable-element domain. After ISO: the ortholog carries one.'],
            ['smed, nvec', '', 'The species whose genes the name was taken from -- this species (another annotation of '
                . 'it) or a related one: smed = Schmidtea mediterranea, nvec = Nematostella vectensis.'],
        ],
        // Checks on the name. Each compares the gene with the human gene it is NAMED after, not with
        // whatever it matches best. In the data (2026-11-24): sim and pthr only on ISO (sim~ also on
        // ISM); tree+ also on ISS; the oma marks on every kind (a later rule named the gene).
        'support' => [
            ['sim+', 'similarity agrees', 'The named human gene is this protein\'s best human match.'],
            ['sim~', 'similarity partly agrees', 'The named gene matches, but another human gene matches better -- '
                . 'common for close paralogs, and not a contradiction by itself. On a family or domain name (ISM): '
                . 'the gene has only a partial human match.'],
            ['sim-', 'no similarity', 'No match to the named gene.'],
            ['pthr+', 'PANTHER agrees', 'The gene\'s own PANTHER family is the same as that of the human gene it is named after.'],
            ['pthrC', 'PANTHER Conflicts', 'The gene\'s own PANTHER family differs from that of the human gene it is named after.'],
            ['tree+', 'tree agrees', 'The PANTHER tree places the gene with the named human gene.'],
            ['treeC', 'tree Conflicts', 'The PANTHER tree places the gene with other human genes.'],
            ['hog', 'Hierarchical Orthologous Group', 'OMA\'s gene family grouping agrees.'],
            ['omaX', 'OMA eXcluded', 'OMA called a human ortholog, but nothing else supported it, so it was set aside '
                . 'and a later rule named the gene.'],
            ['omaC', 'OMA Conflict', 'OMA\'s human ortholog was not used: the gene\'s best human match is another gene '
                . 'AND its PANTHER family differs.'],
            ['omaR', 'OMA Rejected', 'OMA paired many genes here with one human gene and fewer than half passed the '
                . 'checks; none is named after it.'],
        ],
        // The last character of a check, one meaning everywhere.
        'marks' => [
            ['+', 'agrees'], ['~', 'partly: similar, but not the best'], ['C', 'Conflicts: the evidence points elsewhere'],
            ['-', 'no evidence'], ['X', 'eXcluded: set aside'], ['R', 'Rejected: a whole pairing'],
        ],
    ];
}

/**
* Does this directory hold a gene set?
*
* Answered by "does it contain any configured sequence FASTA", because the FASTA is the
* payload — a gene-set directory without one has nothing to serve. Verified against the
* live tree 2026-07-16: 94 dirs have both a FASTA and geneset.json, 0 have only one, so
* either marker works and this one needs no extra metadata file.
*
* Do NOT go back to testing for the GFF. That is what this replaced, and it was circular:
* a gene set with no genes.gff was declared "not a real gene_set dir" and vanished from
* the checks — 23 of the 94 on this deployment have no GFF (protein-only sets legitimately
* have none; JBrowse annotations simply are not available for them). Using the GFF to
* decide what IS a gene set means the ones missing it can never be reported.
*
* 'genome' is excluded: genome.fa lives at the ASSEMBLY level, so including it would make
* every assembly directory look like a gene set.
*/

usages.context: if (!is_gene_set_dir($gs_dir)) continue; // not a gene_set dir

functions.name: moop_find_executable

/**
* Absolute path to a command-line tool, or '' if it cannot be found.
*
* PATH first, then /usr/local/bin and /usr/bin. Both php-fpm's PATH and sudo's secure_path
* routinely leave out /usr/local/bin, which is where htslib, samtools and BLAST land when
* built from source -- so a bare `bgzip` that works in your shell can be "command not
* found" for the web server. That is how six gene tracks were emptied on 2026-10-13
* (`sudo -u apache php scripts/run_housekeeping.php`). Resolve first, and refuse to start
* work that needs a tool you could not find.
*
* An absolute path is used as given when it is executable.
*/

functions.name: moop_parse_source_names
functions.comment:
/**
* The annotation-source filter a search request carries, as a list of exact source names.
*
* Sent as a JSON array: `["Ensembl Homo sapiens", "Closest human gene (Ensembl, no HGNC record)"]`.
* It used to be one comma-joined string split on ',' and each piece trim()med, which broke on two
* real names (2026-10-20):
*   - "Closest human gene (Ensembl, no HGNC record)" -- the gene-naming pipeline's own output --
*     split in two, so filtering by it matched nothing;
*   - eight databases named their RBBH sources "Ensembl Danio rerio " (trailing space), the only
*     difference from the Homologs source; trim() turned every one into the Homologs name, so
*     a filtered search returned no RBBH rows for those organisms.
* Names are matched EXACTLY as stored; normalising them is the loader's job, not the request's.
*
* A plain comma string is still accepted (a page open in a browser from before the change sends
* one) and logged, so we can tell when it is safe to drop.
*
* @return list<string>
*/

* A small (i) button carrying help for ONE field or control.
*
* For the case where a reader is mid-task and must not lose their place. Hard cap of
* roughly 40 words, no tables, no lists longer than three items — if the content does
* not fit that, it was never field help; it belongs in a help_modal() card or in docs/.
*
* Three deliberate choices:
*
* - It is a real <button>, not a styled <span>. That makes it keyboard-focusable and
*   reliably tappable on touch with no tabindex hack, and it announces as a control.
* - Trigger is "focus", not "hover". Hover help is invisible on touch devices and
*   undiscoverable everywhere else; click/tap/keyboard-focus opens it and a click

functions.name: page_purpose
functions.comment:
/**
* The one sentence saying what a page is FOR — rendered on the page, and extractable.
*
* Answers two needs with one declaration, which is the whole point:
*   1. A visitor landing cold sees, in plain language, what this page does.
*   2. `scripts/extract_page_purposes.php` reads it back off the RENDERED page to build
*      the "which page do I want?" router, so the router can never describe a page that
*      no longer says that — or exist for a page that was deleted.
*
* ⚠️ Declared IN THE PAGE, deliberately, not in a config file. A sentence kept somewhere
* else is a sentence nobody updates when the page changes: the description and the page
* drift apart, and only the config gets read. Putting it in the page means editing the
* page IS editing the description.
*
* ⚠️ Extraction reads the rendered HTML, not the source. A grep over source cannot tell
* whether a page still renders a line, or renders it conditionally — the same lesson that
* cost three false findings elsewhere this session (CLAUDE.md §12b).
*
* Keep it to ONE sentence, in the user's language, and say what you get rather than what
* the machinery does: "Compare a sequence against one or more assemblies", not "runs BLAST
* against selected databases".
*
* ⚠️ WRITE IT TO READ IN A LIST, NOT ONLY ON THE PAGE. These sentences are collected onto a
* single "which page do I want?" router, where the reader is NOT standing on the page — so
* "Search genes within THIS assembly" has no referent and reads as a bug. Say "a single
* assembly", "one organism", "a curated group". The four browse pages were written the
* deictic way first and had to be redone; it is easy to miss because on the page itself the
* wrong version reads perfectly well. Avoid this / these / here / above / below.
*
* @param string $text  the sentence
* @param string $extra additional classes for spacing on a particular page
*/

parameters.name: extra
parameters.description: additional classes for spacing on a particular page

functions.name: housekeeping_is_running
functions.comment:
/**
* Is a run in flight right now? True while some process holds the flock on the lock file.
*
* flock, not "is the PID in the file alive": the kernel drops a flock the moment its process
* exits, HOWEVER it exits. The PID test failed both ways at once on 2026-10-30. A background run
* died part-way (fetchData() die()s on a query error), so it never reached the unlink; and
* php-fpm never reaped the child, so the zombie kept /proc/<pid> alive. Every Rebuild click then
* answered "already running" and the hourly sweep never ran, until the fpm worker was recycled.
* Same design as the BLAST queue (lib/blast_queue.php): nothing to clean up, nothing to go stale.
*
* The dashboard uses this to tell the admin "running in the background — your numbers
* will be current next visit", which is the honest way to present the async trade.
*/

usages.context: ok(housekeeping_is_running(), 'while another process holds the lock: running');
ok(!housekeeping_is_running(), 'the holder died without releasing anything: no longer running');
ok(!housekeeping_is_running(), 'a PID in the file means nothing without the flock (the zombie case)');

functions.name: housekeeping_lock_acquire
functions.comment:
/**
* Take the run lock for this process. Returns the handle (keep it open for the whole run), or
* null if another run holds it. If the lock file cannot be opened at all the run goes ahead
* unlocked — a housekeeping that never runs is worse than one that might overlap.
*/

usages.context: ok(housekeeping_lock_acquire() === null, 'a second run is refused while it is held');

functions.name: housekeeping_is_due
housekeeping_requested_at
run_housekeeping
functions.comment:
/**
* AUTO PATH — called from admin_init.php on every admin page load.
*
* Hydrates the session cheaply, then, if due, launches the work in a DETACHED BACKGROUND
* PROCESS and returns immediately. It must never block: this sits in the request path of
* every admin page, and the work is ~4.5s (permission_check alone is ~4.4s of it). Before
* 2026-07-16 this ran the tasks INLINE, so every ~4h one unlucky admin paid 4.5 seconds
* for a page they just wanted to glance at — and admin_init.php's comment claimed it was
* "non-blocking", which is presumably why nobody noticed.
*
* Verified from a real web request: proc_open is available under php-fpm, the parent
* returns in ~1ms, the child SURVIVES the request ending, runs as the web user, and
* inherits php-fpm's mount namespace — that last point matters, because clean_temp_files
* targets sys_get_temp_dir() and php-fpm has PrivateTmp=yes. A cron job would see a
* DIFFERENT /tmp and silently clean nothing; a spawned child sees the right one.
*
* Do NOT call proc_close() on the handle: it WAITS for the child to exit, which would
* reintroduce exactly the block this removes (measured: 1ms without, 2020ms with).
*/

* Launch scripts/run_housekeeping.php detached. Returns true if the spawn was accepted.
*
* Invokes a real script file rather than an inline `php -r` string — nested quoting there
* is fragile enough that it silently produced a child which never ran during testing.
*/

functions.name: housekeeping_run_tasks
functions.comment:
/**
* DOES THE WORK, inline and synchronously. Honours the lock (never stampede a run already
* in flight) but does NOT check the interval — callers decide that.
*
* Called by: scripts/run_housekeeping.php (the background child) and
* admin/api/rerun_housekeeping.php (the dashboard's "Run now" button, where blocking is
* correct — the admin asked and is waiting for the answer).
*
* Every run keeps a record (housekeeping_run_save()): when it started, which task it is on,
* when it finished and how each task went. If the process ends part-way -- die(), a fatal
* error -- a shutdown function writes WHICH task it died in and the message. A process killed
* outright (SIGKILL, out of memory) cannot write anything; housekeeping_health() reads its
* "running" record with no lock held as dead. Until 2026-10-30 a run that died left no trace
* at all (the background child's output goes to /dev/null) and the card still said "Last run
* 12 min ago", because that time was stamped when a run STARTED.
*
* @param list<string> $only Task names to run. Empty = the full sweep. Unknown names are
*                           ignored; if nothing survives filtering the run is refused with
*                           reason 'no_such_task' rather than silently doing nothing.
* @param ?array $registry   Tasks to choose from; null = housekeeping_task_registry(). For tests.
* @return array{ran:bool, reason:?string, tasks:list<array{name:string,ok:bool,ms:int,error:?string}>}
*/

functions.name: housekeeping_health
functions.comment:
/**
* Is housekeeping healthy? Read from the run records alone, so it is cheap and testable.
*
*   danger  a run died (or stopped with no lock held -- killed) and no full sweep has finished
*           since; or a full sweep was requested over 15 minutes ago and none has finished since
*   warn    a run has been going for over 15 minutes; or the last full sweep had failed tasks
*   ''      otherwise
*
* Staleness is measured from the last REQUEST (the marker's mtime), not from the clock.
* Housekeeping only runs while someone uses the admin pages, so "no run for 18 hours" after a
* quiet night is normal, not a failure -- until 2026-11-03 that alone turned the banner red
* every morning, and an alarm that cries wolf daily is ignored the day a run really dies. A
* request that produced no finished sweep within 15 minutes is the real failure (the child
* never started, or never wrote a record). With no request time known, fall back to age.
*
* @param list<array> $runs          the 'housekeeping_runs' records, newest first
* @param bool        $running       housekeeping_is_running()
* @param ?int        $requested_at  housekeeping_requested_at(): when a full sweep was last asked for
* @return array{tone:string, badge:array{0:string,1:string}, headline:string, problems:list<string>}
*/

parameters.name: requested_at
parameters.description: housekeeping_requested_at(): when a full sweep was last asked for

usages.context: ok(housekeeping_health([$_ok($_now - 3 * 3600)], false, $_now)['tone'] === 'danger', 'no full run finished for 3 h (hourly) -> red');
ok(housekeeping_health([$_ok($_now - 600, 'jbrowse_indexes'), $_ok($_now - 3 * 3600)], false, $_now)['tone'] === 'danger', 'a targeted run does not count as a full one');
ok(housekeeping_health([$_ok($_now - 1800)], false, $_now)['tone'] === '', 'a full run 30 min ago -> quiet');
ok(housekeeping_health([['id' => 'r', 'scope' => 'all', 'started_at' => $_now - 60, 'outcome' => 'running'], $_ok($_now - 3000)], true, $_now)['tone'] === '', 'running for a minute -> quiet');
ok(housekeeping_health([], false, $_now)['tone'] === '', 'no record at all (a fresh install, before its first run) -> no false alarm');
ok(housekeeping_health([$_ok($_now - 18 * 3600)], false, $_now, $_now - 18 * 3600)['tone'] === '', 'idle 18 h, nothing requested since the last run -> quiet');
ok(housekeeping_health([$_ok($_now - 18 * 3600)], false, $_now, $_now - 5)['tone'] === '', 'a run requested 5 s ago (this page load) -> quiet, not "18 hr" red');
ok(housekeeping_health([], false, $_now, $_now - 1800)['tone'] === '', 'requested but no record at all -> fresh-install rule still applies');

/**
* Aggregate the filesystem-permission checks into a small severity summary for the
* dashboard pointer card (PAGE_BY_PAGE_AUDIT_PLAN §N).
*
* The underlying scan stat()s the whole organism tree, so it must NOT run on every
* dashboard load — this runs it at most once per HOUSEKEEPING_MIN_INTERVAL and stores
* only the counts. The dashboard reads the cached summary (hydrated into $_SESSION)
* and links to the full Filesystem Permissions page for detail. Uses the SAME shared
* collector the detail page uses, so the numbers always agree.
*
* Persisted to logs/.housekeeping_status.json (next to env_warnings / site_data_backup),
* NOT to cache_path — this is dashboard status, not a regenerable data cache.
*
* NOTE (§O): as of Phase 1 organisms/ is writable again, so a plain permission check
* is accurate. If Phase 2 re-tightens organisms/ to read-only for httpd_t, revisit so
* this doesn't false-alarm on an intentionally read-only tree.
*/

functions.name: housekeeping_check_jbrowse_indexes
functions.comment:
/**
* Count JBrowse gene sets whose registration is out of step with their genes.gff
* (gene_set_jbrowse_problems() -- the one rule): the gene track's bgzip/tabix index, the two
* coordinate files, and the search index.
*
* WHY THIS EXISTS. data/genomes/{org}/{asm}/{gs}/annotations.gff3 is a SYMLINK into
* organisms/, so it silently follows every gene-set reload -- while annotations.gff3.gz,
* which is what JBrowse actually reads, is a snapshot that only changes when someone
* re-preps it by hand. Nothing tied the two together, so a reload staled the browser
* track and said nothing. On 2026-07-29 that was 41 of 69 tracks, some two months
* behind; the two Bradypodion gene sets were serving feature IDs that no longer existed
* in the database at all, so every gene-page link into JBrowse missed.
*
* Until 2026-10-21 only the track index was checked: the search index was never counted
* (none existed, and nothing said so), and coordinate files that failed to rebuild while the
* track was fine were invisible.
*
* Counting is stat calls only. REBUILDING (since 2026-10-13, user's decision) happens first,
* and ONLY in the background run (PHP_SAPI 'cli', scripts/run_housekeeping.php): it
* re-compresses GFFs that can exceed 100 MB, which must never happen inside a page request
* -- and housekeeping still runs inline from the admin "re-run" button and when a spawn
* fails. It used to report only, on the grounds that rebuilding "belongs behind a button";
* the button existed, and 42 of 68 tracks were stale anyway.
*
* Summary: 'need' = gene sets with any problem. 'stale'/'missing'/'broken' count TRACK index
* problems only (a broken track shows no genes at all); 'coords' and 'search' count gene sets
* with that part out of date.
*/

functions.name: housekeeping_gene_set_jbrowse_problems
functions.comment:
/**
* gene_set_jbrowse_problems() for every registered gene set, keyed "org/asm/gs".
* A dangling annotations.gff3 symlink means the gene set is gone, not stale: skipped.
*
* @return array<string, list<array>>
*/

functions.name: housekeeping_rebuild_stale_gene_indexes
functions.comment:
/**
* Bring gene sets back in step with their genes.gff -- broken tracks first, then smallest
* GFF first -- until $budget_seconds is spent; the rest wait for the next run (hourly), so a
* large backlog is worked through without any one run holding the housekeeping lock for long.
* A broken track shows no genes at all; a stale one shows old ones.
*
* "Missing" includes a gene set with no .gz at all. That used to be skipped as "never
* registered -- an admin decision", but annotations.gff3 is only ever created by
* prepareGeneSetForJBrowse() itself, so the symlink existing means registration was
* attempted and the compression step is what failed.
*
* Each gene set gets the manager's own Re-prep: prepareGeneSetForJBrowse() (not forced, so it
* rebuilds only the track index and coordinate files that are out of date and leaves the track
* config alone), then the search index when that part is still out of date. Success means
* gene_set_jbrowse_problems() finds nothing afterwards -- not that each step returned true.
*
* @return array{done: list<string>, failed: list<string>, left: int, seconds: int}
*         failed entries are "org/asm/gs — reason".
*/
functions.returnDescription: list<string>, failed: list<string>, left: int, seconds: int}

functions.name: housekeeping_refresh_organism_cache_if_stale
functions.comment:
/**
* Keep organisms/.organism_cache.json from going stale indefinitely.
*
* Until this task existed, nothing refreshed this cache automatically — only a
* manual "Update Cache" click on the admin dashboard did. That's the same
* silent-staleness trap as PHP sessions: if no admin happens to click it, the
* DB/filesystem drift checks that read from this cache (e.g. gene_set
* directories orphaned by a DB rebuild — see validateAssemblyDirectories())
* never get re-evaluated, so the dashboard can show a clean bill of health
* that's actually days old.
*
* Launches the same background scanner the manual button uses (see
* admin/api/refresh_organism_cache.php) — non-blocking, returns immediately.
* The scan itself only re-examines organisms whose fingerprint changed, so
* this stays cheap even with many organisms.
*
* TRIGGER IS FINGERPRINT-BASED, NOT TIME-BASED. It fires when the per-organism
* fingerprints or the config fingerprint no longer match what the cache was built from —
* i.e. when something ACTUALLY changed — and skips when a scan is already running (lock).
* There is no interval check here despite the function name. (This docblock previously
* claimed "only fires if the cache is older than the refresh interval", and the log line
* below said "12h interval"; both were leftovers from an older time-based version and
* described a gate that does not exist. Corrected 2026-07-16.)
*/

* exits immediately if < 30 days old. No network call happens here.
* If an update is due, launches sync_ncbi_taxonomy_dump.php as a background
* process (same pattern as the organism cache refresh) and returns instantly.
*
* The background script fetches the 50-byte NCBI MD5, compares it, and only
* re-downloads the ~60 MB dump when it has actually changed.
*/

* checksums -- is cheap and runs every pass. The OSV lookup is a network call, so at most
* weekly, like jbrowse_version; sooner when the inventory changed (a library was upgraded,
* so last week's answer is about a version no longer shipped) or when started on its own
* (--task=library_advisories). Only package names and versions leave the server.
* If OSV cannot be reached the last answer is kept and marked, never replaced by "none found".
*/

functions.name: housekeeping_check_security_updates
functions.comment:
/**
* Pending OS security updates -- the check that would have caught PHP2Shell.
*
* PHP2Shell (2026-10-21) was patched only because someone read an article. This host runs
* RHEL's PHP 8.0, which upstream no longer supports: fixes arrive only as Red Hat backports,
* so the version number never looks new and nothing on the site watched the errata. When
* this was written the host had 121 security advisories pending, nginx and OpenSSL among them.
*
* The web server usually may NOT ask the package manager: under SELinux httpd_t cannot open
* the RPM database ("rpmdb open failed", tested 2026-10-22). So the source is a report root
* writes daily into the cache directory (scripts/install_security_report.sh -- a systemd
* timer), and this task only READS it: cheap, so it runs every housekeeping pass.
* Without a report it tries the package manager directly (fine on a host without that
* policy), only in the background CLI run, at most daily; if that fails too, the result
* says how to set the report up rather than claiming "no updates".
*
* Report-only, never installs: that needs root, and updating PHP restarts php-fpm.
*/

functions.name: moop_read_security_report

* card went on listing installed updates and a restart already done for up to an hour after the
* report itself said otherwise (2026-10-27). The running kernel is asked of this machine, not
* taken from the report, so a restart shows as soon as it has happened.
*/

moop_human_check_config
functions.comment:
/**
* Cloudflare Turnstile — "is this a person?" once per browser session, for anonymous visitors.
*
* Why: AI-training crawlers request every URL they can find, from thousands of IPs, and ignore
* robots.txt. Each gene page is several SQLite queries; each export or download is far more.
* A challenge a real browser passes invisibly — and a mass crawler cannot afford — stops them
* before any data code runs. Plan and layers: notes/BOT_PROTECTION_PLAN.md.
*
* Who is checked: anonymous visitors only. Logged-in users never are, and internal/VPN
* addresses are auto-logged-in by access_control.php (auto_login_ip_ranges), so they never
* are either.
*
* If Cloudflare cannot be reached (server side), the visitor is let in for
* HUMAN_CHECK_FAILOPEN_TTL and asked again after (Sofia, 2026-10-28: keep the site up for real
* users; the nginx rate limits are the backstop for that window). A visitor can never claim
* an outage — only this server's own failed call to Cloudflare counts as one.
*
* History: the first version (cd1b8161, June 2026) called /turnstile/v1/, which does not exist
* (only v0 does), so it could never have verified anyone; and its page was then deleted as dead
* code (ac0ce979) while the redirect to it stayed live — enabling Turnstile would have sent
* every anonymous visitor to a 404.
*/

const HUMAN_CHECK_PASS_TTL     = 12 * 3600;  // a pass lasts the working day
const HUMAN_CHECK_FAILOPEN_TTL = 10 * 60;    // a Cloudflare outage lets people in, briefly
const HUMAN_CHECK_SITEVERIFY   = 'https://challenges.cloudflare.com/turnstile/v0/siteverify';
const HUMAN_CHECK_SCRIPT       = 'https://challenges.cloudflare.com/turnstile/v0/api.js';

/** Turnstile settings, or null when it is off or not fully configured. */

* Did this track JSON come from a Google Sheet?
