/**
* A track's metadata as the BROWSER should see it: what describes the data, flattened so
* JBrowse can filter on it. The stored track JSON is left as it is.
*
* JBrowse's faceted track selector (Available tracks -> menu -> faceted view) makes one
* filter column per TOP-LEVEL metadata key and skips any value that is an object; its search
* box does the same. Everything that describes a track lives in ONE nested object --
* google_sheets_metadata (technique, source, project, experiment, developmental_stage, tissue,
* condition, citation, ...) -- so until 2026-10-23 none of it could be filtered or searched,
* and the columns JBrowse did offer were internal bookkeeping (file path, access level,
* management id, remote flag, date added). On Nematostella that is 966 RNA-seq tracks in one
* flat "Gene Expression" folder with nothing to narrow them by.
*
* Here the sheet's fields are lifted to the top level (blank ones dropped, runs of whitespace
* collapsed), a non-empty description and read counts are kept, and the internal keys are left
* out. The admin track-details view reads the stored file, so it still shows everything.
* The sheet stays the source of truth for the values: no synonyms are merged here.
*/

functions.name: moop_log_index_build

/**
* One log line for an index build, saying plainly when it did NOT work.
*
* ⚠️ This exists because both index builds used to be written as
*
*     } elseif (generateFooIndex($path)) {
*         $log[] = "generated foo.tsv";
*     }
*
* with no else -- so a FALSE return logged nothing at all and registration
* reported success. The gene set then looked fully registered while the feature
* quietly did not work, which is this codebase's most repeated failure shape:
* a write the web server could not do, unchecked, reported as success.
*
* An EMPTY file is treated as a failure too. The generators return true once
* they have opened their input and output, so a GFF with no exon features
* produces a zero-byte index and a cheerful "generated" line -- green status,
* missing feature.
*
* @param bool $ok What the generator returned.
* @param string $consequence What breaks if this index is missing, in plain words.
*/

functions.name: unregisterAssembly
functions.comment:
/**
* Unregister an assembly from JBrowse: remove every artifact that registration created,
* and nothing else. The inverse of admin/api/jbrowse_register_assembly.php.
*
* This NEVER touches organisms/ (taking data off the site is lib/retire.php's job). Registration
* only ever creates derived artifacts (a data/genomes/ directory holding a symlink into
* organisms/, plus a registry JSON), so unregistering only ever removes derived artifacts.
* The source data is left exactly as it is — that is what makes this safe to offer as a
* one-click admin action, and re-registering afterwards is cheap.
*
* Intended for the registrations reported by getOrphanedJBrowseRegistrations(): source data
* renamed or removed outside MOOP, leaving a dangling reference.fasta that serves HTTP 404.
*
* Track JSONs are preserved if any exist — those represent real curation work, and an
* assembly can be re-registered under the correct name without rebuilding them. Only the
* empty directory skeleton is cleaned up.
*
* @return array ['success'=>bool, 'error'=>string?, 'removed'=>string[], 'kept'=>string[]]
*/

functions.name: buildGeneSetTextIndex
functions.comment:
/**
* Run jbrowse text-index for a specific gene set and update its track JSON.
* Trix files go in data/genomes/{organism}/{assembly}/{gene_set}/trix/ (moop_jbrowse_trix_location()).
*
* @return array ['success'=>bool, 'error'=>string?, ...]
*/

functions.name: generateExonCoordsIndex
functions.comment:
/**
* Build exon_coords.tsv from a sorted GFF3 file.
*
* Sibling of generateFeatureCoordsIndex(), and deliberately the same shape:
* streamed, flushed one gene family at a time, regenerated at registration.
* Where feature_coords.tsv gives a feature's OUTER span, this gives a
* transcript's EXON STRUCTURE — the thing an outer span cannot express.
*
* It exists so a hit in transcript coordinates can be mapped back to the genome.
* A primer sitting across an exon junction has no continuous genomic match, so it
* can only be drawn correctly as two blocks, and that split needs the exon
* boundaries. Reading them from the GFF on demand is not viable: Nematostella's
* genes.gff is 240 MB and a filtered pass costs about a second per search.
*
* Output: transcript_id \t chr \t strand \t start,end \t s1,e1;s2,e2;...
*
* Rows are emitted for the GFF ID and for the id with its source prefix stripped
* (moop_gff_bare_id(): rna-, transcript:, ...), because the database and FASTA
* headers carry the bare accession while the GFF carries "rna-ACC" — looking up
* one by the other silently finds nothing. This used its own rna-/cds-/gene-/id-
* list, which missed Ensembl's "transcript:", so no Drosophila transcript could
* be placed on the genome.
*
* No list of transcript types is used. Anything that ends up with exon children
* is treated as a transcript, so lncRNA, tRNA and pseudogenic_transcript are
* handled without being enumerated — a type list is exactly what makes this class
* of script quietly skip whole categories of gene.
*/

functions.name: generateFeatureCoordsIndex
functions.comment:
/**
* Build feature_coords.tsv from a sorted GFF3 file.
*
* Streams the file one line at a time. Because the GFF is coordinate-sorted
* (by our bgzip prep step), all children of a gene appear consecutively after
* the gene line. When a new root feature is encountered the previous gene's
* batch is flushed to disk — so only one gene family is in memory at a time.
*
* Output format: hit_id\tgene_id\tchr\tstart\tend\tstrand
*/

functions.name: moop_bgzf_is_complete
functions.comment:
/**
* Is this a complete, non-empty BGZF file (a bgzipped GFF, or a tabix .tbi/.csi)?
*
* Reads 4 bytes at the start and 28 at the end: the BGZF header and the EOF block. Cheap
* enough to run on every gene track every housekeeping interval, and it catches the states
* an mtime cannot: a 0-byte file, an interrupted write, a plain-gzip or uncompressed file.
* A file that is ONLY the EOF block (28 bytes) is an empty archive, so it fails too.
*/

functions.name: gene_track_index_problem
functions.comment:
/**
* What, if anything, is wrong with a gene track's compressed GFF and tabix index.
*
* THE single rule. The dashboard count (housekeeping), the background rebuild's work list,
* the prep step and the gene page's tabix fast path (lib/gff_gene_model.php) all call this.
* It used to be written out five times, and the copies drifted.
*
* @param string $gff  data/genomes/{org}/{asm}/{gs}/annotations.gff3 (the symlink).
* @return array{kind: 'missing'|'stale'|'broken', why: string}|null  null = sound and current.
*/
functions.returnDescription: 'missing'|'stale'|'broken', why: string}|null  null = sound and current.

functions.name: gene_set_jbrowse_problems
functions.comment:
/**
* Everything a gene set's JBrowse registration derives from its genes.gff, and what is wrong
* with each part -- the one answer to "does this gene set need a Re-prep?".
*
*   track   annotations.gff3.gz + tabix index      gene_track_index_problem()
*   coords  feature_coords.tsv, exon_coords.tsv    missing, or older than genes.gff (the same
*                                                  test prepareGeneSetForJBrowse() rebuilds on)
*   search  trix/annotations.gff3.gz.ix            missing, older than the .gz it indexes, not
*                                                  linked from the track, or built with other
*                                                  attributes than MOOP_JBROWSE_TEXT_INDEX_ATTRIBUTES
*
* Only the first of these used to be checked. A new genes.gff therefore staled the coordinates
* and the search index with nothing saying so, and no gene set had a search index at all
* (2026-10-21) without any page noticing. Stat calls plus one small JSON read: cheap enough
* for housekeeping and for Manage JBrowse to run live.
*
* @param string $gff        data/genomes/{org}/{asm}/{gs}/annotations.gff3 (the symlink)
* @param string $track_json the gene track's config; '' skips the two checks that need it
* @return list<array{part: 'track'|'coords'|'search', kind: 'missing'|'stale'|'broken', why: string}>
*         empty = current
*/

parameters.name: track_json
parameters.description: the gene track's config; '' skips the two checks that need it

functions.name: gene_track_build_index
functions.comment:
/**
* Sort + bgzip + tabix a gene track, replacing the live files only once the new ones are
* verified. Returns false (and logs why) without touching the live files on any failure.
*
* The order is the point. This used to unlink the old .gz/.tbi FIRST and then run
* `... | bgzip > annotations.gff3.gz`. On 2026-10-13 `sudo -u apache` ran it with a PATH
* lacking /usr/local/bin: the shell created the output file, bgzip was "command not found",
* and six tracks were left as 0-byte files -- newer than their GFF, so nothing noticed.
* Now: (1) resolve bgzip and tabix to absolute paths before anything else, (2) build into a
* temp name beside the target, under pipefail, (3) check the result is complete BGZF and
* that tabix indexed it, (4) rename into place. A failed run leaves what was there.
*/

functions.name: moop_jwt_key_paths
functions.comment:
/**
* Where the JWT key pair lives: <moop>/certs/. Every reader goes through here -- signing and
* verifying below, the permissions check, housekeeping, setup and setup-check, the tracks
* server admin page -- so a check can never inspect a different file from the one in use.
*
* Fixed, not configured, on purpose: this file also runs on the tracks server, which has no
* MOOP config to read a path from. Until 2026-10-23 site_config.php carried six settings
* (certs_directory, jwt_private_key, jwt_public_key, twice over) that LOOKED like they moved
* the keys; the signing code never read any of them, so changing one would only have pointed
* the health checks at the wrong file.
*
* The directory is inside the web root. nginx refuses it outright (location ^~ /moop/certs/
* in docs/nginx/moop-security.conf); the 2750 directory mode is the second line, not the only one.
*
* @return array{dir: string, private: string, public: string}
*/

usages.context: require_once __DIR__ . '/jbrowse/track_token.php';   // moop_jwt_key_paths(): the keys signing really uses

generateTrackToken

* Generate JWT token for track access
*
* Token design (2026-07-13): each token is bound to the ONE file it authorizes, via
* the `file` claim (the exact `?file=` path tracks.php will receive, e.g.
* "Organism/Assembly/type/reads.bam"). tracks.php serves a file only if the token's
* `file` matches the requested one, so a token handed out for a PUBLIC file cannot be
* replayed against a COLLABORATOR file on the same assembly — the authorization rides
* in the signed token itself, so the tracks server needs no access list of its own.
* organism/assembly are kept for logging/context; the security check is on `file`.
* Still no user_id (avoids username leakage to external servers).
*
* @param string $organism

* logic in four places, discovering the same bug four times.

* This returns the RAW traversal — every visited node, tagged with the seed it came from and
* its depth. Callers post-process into whatever shape they need; the graph walk itself is
* not their business.

*   - `f.feature_id <> c.feature_id` stops a SELF-PARENT. Schmidtea_lugubris carried 14,313
*     of these before its 2026-08-05 reload, and most databases are still unreloaded.
*   - `depth < MOOP_HIERARCHY_MAX_DEPTH` stops a MULTI-ROW cycle, which the first guard
*     cannot see.
* SQLite 3.34.1 here has no `CYCLE` clause, so this is done by hand. Without them the query
* does not error — it pins a php-fpm worker until the request times out.
*
* @param string[] $seeds        feature_uniquename values to start from
* @param string   $dbFile       path to organism.sqlite
* @param string   $direction    'up' (ancestors, default) or 'down' (descendants)

functions.name: amplifiableKb
functions.comment:
/**
* Largest product standard PCR realistically makes, in bp.
*
* Distinct from MAX_PRODUCT_DEFAULT, which governs what is REPORTED. This
* governs what COUNTS: a real 8 kb off-target is still listed because it
* exists, but it will not amplify under normal conditions and so must not turn
* an otherwise clear pair ambiguous.
*
* 3 kb (was 2 kb until 2026-10-13, user's call after checking). Taq works best
* under 2 kb but is dependable to about 3 kb; past 3-4 kb products need
* optimisation or a long-range polymerase (Qiagen Taq product page and bench
* guide). Every user-facing mention of the limit is computed from this constant
* via amplifiableKb(), so the wording cannot drift from the rule.
*/
const AMPLIFIABLE_MAX = 3000;

/** AMPLIFIABLE_MAX for display: "3" (or "2.5"). */

usages.context: . 'is dependable for products under ' . PrimerPairs::amplifiableKb() . ' kb; longer ones often amplify poorly '
'text'  => t('A product is listed, but it is longer than %s kb.', PrimerPairs::amplifiableKb())
. ' ' . t('Standard PCR is dependable for products under %s kb; longer ones often amplify poorly or not at all, so it is not counted.', PrimerPairs::amplifiableKb())
'' . t('under %s kb', PrimerPairs::amplifiableKb()) . '', $b("last 5 bases of the 3′ end"))
'how_to_read' => 'A product would amplify when it is under ' . PrimerPairs::amplifiableKb() . ' kb, each primer has fewer than 6 '
ok(PrimerPairs::amplifiableKb() === '3', 'the limit is shown as "3" kb');

functions.name: isAmplifiable
functions.comment:
/**
* Would standard PCR make this product?
*
* Three conditions, in the order they matter:
*   1. short enough to amplify at all;
*   2. neither primer so mismatched that the site is implausible;
*   3. neither primer blocked at its 3' end.
*
* Condition 3 is the one a mismatch COUNT cannot express, and it is the one
* that decides most real cases.
*/

functions.name: findProducts
functions.comment:
/**
* Find every product a pair's hits could form on a single database.
*
* @param array $hits    ['forward' => [...], 'reverse' => [...]] from PrimerBlast.
* @param array $options ['max_product' => int]
* @return array {
*     @type array $products      Each: subject, start, end, size, primers, mismatch info.
*     @type int   $product_count
*     @type array $primer_hits   ['forward' => n, 'reverse' => n]
*     @type array $paired_hits   How many of those matches actually ended up in a
*                                product. The difference is matches that found no
*                                partner -- which is the normal fate of most of them,
*                                and needs saying, or a user who RAISES a limit sees
*                                the match count rise with nothing to show for it.
*     @type int   $over_max      Combinations discarded by the size bound.
*     @type string|null $carried_by  'forward'|'reverse' when specificity rests on one primer.
* }
*/

functions.name: wouldPrime
functions.comment:
/**
* Would both primers bind well enough to prime here, whatever the distance?
*
* isAmplifiable() without its length test. It separates a REAL locus that is merely
* long (a perfect 6,389 bp product across introns) from a site that only looks like
* one (a junction primer's half-match in the genome: 3 mismatches, never primes).
*/

functions.name: realLocus
functions.comment:
/**
* The pair's real locus on this database: the primary product among sites where
* both primers would prime (wouldPrime()), or null if there is none.
*
* On the genome, for a pair designed on cDNA, this is what "the gDNA product" means.
* primaryProduct() alone picks the closest-looking site even when it could never
* prime, and the page then reported "gDNA 7,906 bp" for a pair whose forward primer
* sits across an exon junction and has no genomic product at all (2026-10-29).
*
* @return array|null
*/

usages.context: group('PrimerPairs — realLocus(): the genomic product is a site where both primers would prime');

functions.name: primaryProduct
functions.comment:
/**
* The product a user would call "the" product for this pair.
*
* Needed because the genomic-vs-cDNA size comparison (the intron-spanning
* verdict) has to compare LIKE WITH LIKE. Taking products[0] after a sort by
* size is wrong: a self-pairing artefact that happens to be smaller than the
* real amplicon would silently become the number the verdict is computed from,
* and the verdict would be confidently incorrect.
*
* Preference order: a genuine forward+reverse product, then fewest mismatches,
* then smallest.
*
* @return array|null
*/

usages.context: group('PrimerPairs — primaryProduct() must compare like with like');
ok(PrimerPairs::primaryProduct(['products' => []]) === null, 'no products yields null, not a crash');
ok(PrimerPairs::primaryProduct($junction)['size'] === 7906, 'the closest-looking site is still found (kept as a footnote)');

functions.name: product
functions.comment:
/**
* Would these two hits amplify a fragment between them?
*
* Two conditions, and BOTH are required:
*   1. Opposite strands. Two same-strand hits cannot bracket anything.
*   2. They must FACE each other. A plus-strand primer extends towards higher
*      coordinates, a minus-strand primer towards lower ones, so the plus hit
*      must lie to the LEFT. Reversed, the primers point away and nothing is
*      amplified -- a case that looks like a valid pair on a plain BLAST page.
*
* Note neither hit is assumed to be "the forward primer": on a minus-strand
* gene the user's forward primer aligns to the minus strand. That is exactly
* the measured case, and hard-coding the roles would have missed it.
*/

functions.name: cardParams
validateCard
functions.comment:
/**
* Check and tidy a card from the admin form. Returns [card, errors]. The bounds are
* Primer3Design::OPTIONS -- the same ones Primer Maker's own form enforces -- so a card can never
* hold a number the tool would refuse. min <= opt <= max is checked on the values the card will
* really run with (its own, or the shipped default where left blank).
*
* @param array  $in         label[lang], blurb[lang], size_range, CARD_FIELDS..., tail
* @param array  $langs      the site's language codes; English is required
* @param array  $tail_ids   tag ids that exist (PrimerTails::catalogue)
*/

parameters.name: langs
parameters.description: the site's language codes; English is required

functions.name: catalogue
functions.comment:
/**
* The adapters offered on the page.
*
* Pure on purpose: the caller reads config and passes it in, so this stays
* testable with no ConfigManager and no site data — the same rule
* Primer3Design::buildInput() follows, and for the same reason.
*
* Configured entries REPLACE a built-in with the same id rather than being
* appended beside it, so a deployment that needs a different T4P gets one
* entry rather than two identically-labelled ones.
*
* @param array $configured Entries from the 'primer_tails' config key.
* @return array Keyed by id.
*/

functions.name: normalise
validate
functions.comment:
/**
* Why this sequence cannot be used as a tail, or '' if it can.
*
* An empty tail is valid: it means "no tail on this side", which is a real
* choice when only one primer needs an adapter.
*/

usages.context: ok(PrimerTails::validate('') === '', 'an empty tail is valid — it means no tail on that side');
ok(PrimerTails::validate('ACGTN') !== '', 'N is rejected: an oligo is synthesised exactly as written');
ok(PrimerTails::validate(str_repeat('A', 61)) !== '', 'a tail past the length cap is rejected');
ok(PrimerTails::validate(' acg tac g ') === '', 'whitespace is not a reason to reject a tail');

* @param array  $catalogue  From catalogue().
* @return array ['id','label','forward','reverse','note','errors' => []]

functions.name: apply
functions.comment:
/**
* Add the tailed forms of a primer pair alongside the untailed ones.
*
* ⚠️ ADDS KEYS ONLY. left_sequence and right_sequence keep holding the bare
* primer, because that is what every statistic was computed on and what the
* specificity check has to receive.
*
* @param array $pair From Primer3Design::parseOutput().
* @param array $tail From resolve().
* @return array The pair with tail_* keys added when a tail applies.
*/
functions.returnDescription: The pair with tail_* keys added when a tail applies.

usages.context: <li>Check and apply (a reload finishes the requests in progress; nobody is cut off):
<form method="post"><?= csrf_input_field() ?><input type="hidden" name="_action" value="apply"><input type="hidden" name="lang" value="<?= $h($lang) ?>">
'apply() does NOT touch left_sequence — the checker must receive the untailed primer');

functions.name: reverseComplement
functions.comment:
/**
* Reverse complement, for reading the reverse tag off the top strand.
*
* ⚠️ lib/blast_functions.php defines a reverseComplement() too, and this is
* deliberately not that one: it sits in 1,100 lines of BLAST plumbing that
* the primer libraries otherwise never load, and pulling all of it in to
* borrow a one-liner buys a dependency far heavier than the duplication.
* Tails are validated to A/C/G/T before they reach here (see validate()),
* so the degenerate codes it would also need are not a gap.
*
* @param string $seq Tail sequence.
* @return string
*/

functions.name: oligoRecords
functions.comment:
/**
* Oligos exactly as they should be ordered, for the FASTA and TSV surfaces.
*
* One code path produces every output form. The CGI this replaces had the
* table showing tailed and untailed side by side while the FASTA block below
* it emitted only the untailed form, its tailed branch commented out — so
* the file you downloaded disagreed with the table you were reading.
*
* @param string $record_id Sequence the pairs were designed from.
* @param array  $pairs     Pairs already through apply().
* @param array  $tail      From resolve().
* @return array Each: ['name','sequence','side','rank','tailed','length']
*/

parameters.name: record_id
parameters.description: Sequence the pairs were designed from.

functions.name: parse
functions.comment:
/**
* Read a pasted sequence and separate the DNA from the instructions.
*
* @param string $raw Sequence as typed, FASTA header already removed.
* @return array {
*   @type string $sequence   Bare DNA, upper-cased, no marks, no whitespace.
*   @type array  $junctions  1-based positions K: the junction FOLLOWS base K.
*   @type array  $targets    [[start1, length], …] regions the product must contain.
*   @type array  $errors     Fatal problems; the caller must not design.
*   @type array  $notes      What was found, so a stray mark is never silent.
* }
*/

parameters.name: raw
parameters.description: Sequence as typed, FASTA header already removed.

usages.context: 'parse() warns once, for the forward primer only, and still keeps the pair');
ok($_p13 && $_p13['org'] === 'Nv' && $_p13['disk_kb'] === null && $_p13['db_n'] === 0, 'lines from before the database columns still parse (disk = not measured)');

functions.name: hasMarkup
functions.comment:
/**
* Does this text contain any markup at all?
*
* Used to decide whether the user has said something explicit that should
* beat a looked-up exon index. Cheap, and keeps that decision readable at
* the call site.
*/

usages.context: ok(SequenceMarkup::hasMarkup('ACGT') === false, 'plain sequence reports no markup');
ok(SequenceMarkup::hasMarkup('ACGT|ACGT') === true, 'a junction mark is detected');

functions.name: annotate
functions.comment:
/**
* Put junction marks back INTO a sequence, for display.
*
* The reverse of parse(), so a looked-up exon structure can be shown in the
* box the user is reading rather than described in a sentence beside it.
*
* ⚠️ Not used to feed primer3 — positions stay the source of truth. This is
* for showing a user where the junctions are, and for letting them take the
* marked-up sequence away and edit it.
*
* @param string $sequence  Bare DNA.
* @param array  $junctions 1-based positions K; the mark goes AFTER base K.
*/

parameters.name: junctions
parameters.description: 1-based positions K; the mark goes AFTER base K.

usages.context: ok(SequenceMarkup::annotate('ACGTACGT', [4]) === 'ACGT|ACGT', 'annotate puts a mark after base 4');

* RETIRE / RESTORE AN ORGANISM, ASSEMBLY OR GENE SET — takes it off the site and cleans up what
* MOOP made for it, reversibly. Plan and reasoning: notes/RETIRE_DATA_PLAN.md.
*
* Nothing is deleted. The directory is MOVED (rename) to
* organisms/.retired/<YYYYMMDD-HHMMSS>_<Organism>[__<Assembly>[__<GeneSet>]]/data/ — same
* volume, so instant; already denied by nginx; already writable by the web server. Its JBrowse
* settings are moved into the same bundle; derived JBrowse files are removed (assembly level:
* the registration) or moved with it (gene set level: its built track and search index, so a
* restore needs no rebuild); its group entries are saved in the bundle's retired.json and
* removed; its cache directory (regenerable) is deleted. users.json is never touched, so a
* restore brings people's access back.
*
* ONE DATABASE PER ORGANISM: an assembly or gene set retired here still has rows in
* organism.sqlite until the pipeline rebuilds the database without it. Meanwhile it is hidden
* everywhere because every scope — selectors, downloads, and since this change the search
* endpoint (moop_search_permitted_scope()) — is built from group entries plus directories, and
* it has neither. The health checks list it as "retired, waiting for a database rebuild"
* (validateAssemblyDirectories()'s 'retired' list), not as a missing directory.
*
* Every step is recorded in retired.json AS IT COMPLETES. A failure part-way leaves an exact
* record of what was done, and restore undoes exactly that.
*/

require_once __DIR__ . '/functions_json.php';         // loadJsonFile()
require_once __DIR__ . '/functions_database.php';     // fetchData()

require_once __DIR__ . '/gene_set_identity.php';      // moop_gene_set_identity()
require_once __DIR__ . '/jbrowse/gene_set_functions.php';   // unregisterAssembly(), moop_gene_track_json_path()

/**
* Where the web server writes its temporary files: BLAST results (the raw archive, XML,
* pairwise, tabular), sequence-extraction batch lists, primer and alignment inputs.
*
* Not /tmp. On this host /tmp is a 4 GB volume, and php-fpm's PrivateTmp is only a directory
* on it, so a few large BLAST searches at once could fill it (one left a 374 MB archive and a
* 268 MB XML behind), and then every BLAST and sequence download fails. /var is no better
* (4 GB, 85% full). The big disk is the one holding the web root, so the directory is a
* HIDDEN one beside the app: nginx's moop-security.conf already refuses every path segment
* that starts with a dot, so nothing in it is ever served.
*
* Also unlike PrivateTmp, the command line sees the same directory as php-fpm, so
* housekeeping and an admin at a shell clean and inspect the same files.
*
* Created (apache-owned, mode 2770, SELinux httpd_sys_rw_content_t) by
* scripts/fix_moop_selinux.sh. Until it exists and is writable, this FAILS OPEN to the system
* temp dir, with the reason in the error log: a missing temp directory must never stop a search.
*/

/** The directory MOOP means to use: {web root}/.{site}-tmp, e.g. /var/www/html/.moop-tmp */

usages.context: require_once __DIR__ . '/temp_dir.php';   // moop_temp_dir_path(): the Temp Directory rule

* pairwise, tabular), sequence-extraction batch lists, primer and alignment inputs.

* Not /tmp. On this host /tmp is a 4 GB volume, and php-fpm's PrivateTmp is only a directory
* on it, so a few large BLAST searches at once could fill it (one left a 374 MB archive and a
* 268 MB XML behind), and then every BLAST and sequence download fails. /var is no better
* (4 GB, 85% full). The big disk is the one holding the web root, so the directory is a
* HIDDEN one beside the app: nginx's moop-security.conf already refuses every path segment
* that starts with a dot, so nothing in it is ever served.
*
* Also unlike PrivateTmp, the command line sees the same directory as php-fpm, so
* housekeeping and an admin at a shell clean and inspect the same files.
*
* Created (apache-owned, mode 2770, SELinux httpd_sys_rw_content_t) by
* scripts/fix_moop_selinux.sh. Until it exists and is writable, this FAILS OPEN to the system
* temp dir, with the reason in the error log: a missing temp directory must never stop a search.

/** The directory MOOP means to use: {web root}/.{site}-tmp, e.g. /var/www/html/.moop-tmp */

functions.name: getWikipediaOrganismData
functions.comment:
/**
* Cached organism lookup — THE entry point. Callers must not reach past this.
*
* Keyed by SCIENTIFIC NAME, because the answer is a function of the name and nothing else.
* It used to be keyed by whatever the caller passed first: the organism page passed the
* directory name, the image lookup passed the COMMON name. Nine planarians share the common
* name "Freshwater planarian", so they shared one cache entry — whichever was looked up first
* decided the answer for all nine, and an image found that way is saved permanently under
* each organism's own name. Found 2026-10-28 (13 stray cache directories named after common
* names, e.g. "Cura Pinguis Unknown Species").
*
* An uncached lookup is several sequential calls to Wikipedia, so it must not run unbounded
* inside a page request (measured 2026-08-04: 348 ms of a 428 ms organism page). Three
* guards:
*   - results are cached: 30 days for a hit, 7 for "no article", each stretched by a per-name
*     ±20% so organisms looked up together do not all expire together;
*   - at most WIKI_LOOKUPS_PER_REQUEST live lookups per request. A list page (a group of 49
*     bats) used to look up every uncached organism in one request — on 2026-10-21 ~50 in a
*     single minute — which is how Wikipedia came to refuse them;
*   - a refusal or network failure is NEVER cached. Only a lookup in which every call got a
*     real answer is written. Before 2026-10-28 the HTTP status was not checked, so a refusal
*     read as "no article" and was kept for a week (50 organisms, Myotis lucifugus among them).
* When the budget is spent or Wikipedia cannot be asked, a stale entry beats nothing.
*
* @param string $scientific_name "Genus species"; "Genus sp" gets the genus article
* @param string $common_name     optional; tried as a title, accepted only if the article
*                                names the species (see moop_wikipedia_fetch_organism_uncached)
* @return array description, image_url, wikipedia_url, source, title, and scope
*               ('species' | 'genus' | '' when nothing was found)
*/

parameters.description: "Genus species"; "Genus sp" gets the genus article

parameters.name: common_name

/**
* Wallace rule: 2°C per A/T, 4°C per G/C — the standard estimate at this length.
*
* NOT the salt-adjusted 64.9 + 41*(GC-16.4)/N formula, which is for longer
* oligos: on a 20-mer that one returns 48-56°C across the entire 40-60% GC band,
* so combining it with a 56-64°C window accepts nothing at all. (It did exactly
* that here, and the generator silently produced no output.)
*/

usages.context: printf("    F %s   GC %2.0f%%  Tm %d\n", $d['forward'], gc_pct($d['forward']), tm_wallace($d['forward']));
printf("    R %s   GC %2.0f%%  Tm %d\n", $d['reverse'], gc_pct($d['reverse']), tm_wallace($d['reverse']));

functions.name: section
detectWebUser
functions.comment:
/**
* Detect the web server user/group from running processes.
*
* When this script runs from CLI, posix_getuid() returns the CLI user (e.g.
* ubuntu), not the web server. Instead we inspect running apache2/httpd/nginx/
* php-fpm worker processes (skipping root, which owns the parent process) to
* find the actual web server identity. Falls back to 'www-data' if no web
* server process is detected.
*/

functions.name: detectWebServer
functions.comment:
/**
* Which web server is actually running? MOOP supports both Apache and nginx, so no
* check may assume one. Detected from running processes (same approach as
* detectWebUser), falling back to which config tree exists on disk.
*
* @return string 'nginx' | 'apache' | 'unknown'
*/

functions.name: webUserIds
functions.comment:
/**
* Numeric uid/gid for the web server account. Cached; resolved without posix.
*
* The posix extension is NOT loaded in this PHP CLI (verified 2026-07-16), so
* posix_getpwnam() and friends are unavailable here even though the same functions
* work under php-fpm. Fall back to id/getent.
*
* @return array{uid:?int, gid:?int}
*/

functions.name: webCanWrite
functions.comment:
/**
* Can the WEB SERVER write here? — not "can whoever ran this script write here".
*
* is_writable() answers for the current process. Run as the deploy user (the normal case
* for a preflight) it is owner-biased and wrong in BOTH directions: it says "no" for a
* directory apache owns and can write (observed on archived_gene_sets, apache:apache 755)
* and "yes" for one only the deploy user can write. Predict apache's DAC view from the
* raw mode bits and numeric ids instead.
*
* DAC only. On an enforcing host the SELinux label can still block a write that passes
* here — that is what the SELinux section checks, and it is the more common failure.
*/
